maintopic: FARM CREDIT
FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of bill No. 134, to encourage the provision of intermediate term and short-term credit to farmers for the improvement and development of farms, and for the improvement of living conditions thereon.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
There will not be a chance to discuss the provisions of this bill after it gets second reading because it will be referred to the committee on banicing and commerce, and only this morning we received the printed bill. I wish to make a few observations on it.
As pointed out in the discussion of the resolution, I think it is very important that we should have been able to discuss the legislation pertaining to floor prices of agricultural products in conjunction with this bill. The matter of a central agricultural bank in connection with floor prices will have a distinct bearing on the success or otherwise on the operation of the proposed act.
Paragraph (h) of section 2, the interpretation section, defines "farm improvement loan" as meaning a loan made by a bank to a farmer for the purpose of financing-
(i)	the purchase of agricultural implements;
(ii)	the purchase of live stock;
(iii)	the purchase or installation of agricultural equipment or a farm electric system;
(iv)	the alteration or improvement of a farm electric system;
(v)	the erection or construction of fencing or works for drainage on a farm;
(vi)	the construction, repair or alteration of, or making of additions to, any building or structure on a farm; or
(vii)	any work for the improvement or development of a farm designated in the regulations.

Farm Credit-Mr. Ross (Souris)
I do not see among these items any provision for seed grain. It will be readily realized that the farmer who needs assistance under this legislation may have had a crop failure through no fault of his own. That failure may be caused by hail in the district, and he may not have proper coverage of insurance to protect him. It may be caused by a grasshopper plague or drought in certain sections of the country. There is no provision made for that man to purchase his seed grain.
There is another matter that has been brought up by a colleague of mine in banking and commerce committees of other sessions, namely, a guarantee for binder twine in harvest time. It is recognized that in the prairie provinces binder twine must now be purchased on a cash basis. The farmer must make provision to pay cash for it, but there is no provision in this legislation for that. I am wondering whether those two items should not be included in this bill when it comes before the committee.
I go on with the clauses of the bill. Paragraph (i) of section 2 reads as follows:
"Farmer" means a person who is in possession of a farm and whose principal occupation consists of farming such farm.
When the resolution was under consideration I pointed out that there has been much trouble with the treasury board in the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in the past few years as to what properly constituted a farmer. I think it is important that that should be clearly understood in this measure.
Then, going on to section 3, "Guaranteed farm improvement loans," paragraph (d) subsection 1, reads as follows:
The principal amount of the loan did not at the time of the making of the loan, together with the amount owing in respect of other farm improvement loans previously made to the borrower and disclosed in his application, or of which the bank had knowledge, exceeded the sum of three thousand dollars.
That means, of course, that all other liabilities will be taken into account at the time. In many instances this will prevent a farmer from obtaining credit under this legislation, particularly farmers who have extensive liabilities on their farms.
Paragraph (e) is as follows: the loan was repayable in full by the terms thereof in not more than ten years.
That allows ten years for repayment.
Paragraph (f) states:
the rate of interest charged by the bank on the loan did not exceed five per centum per annum simple interest as long as the borrower wras not in default.
100-231i
In the resolution stage I pointed out that I was distinctly of the opinion that the rate of interest of five per cent was too high. I have pointed out that to-day many good farmers are receiving credit for five per cent. When the resolution was before the committee several other speakers stated that the rate of interest should not exceed the cost of the operation. I have already pointed to the Veterans' Land Settlement Act, where land is being purchased and resold to the veterans and ip costing them three and a half per cent. I suggest that the rate of interest in this bill should not exceed four per cent.
Section 4 deals with the limitations of the amount of the liability to the bank. It is as follows:
The minister shall not be liable under this act to pay to a bank a total amount in excess of ten per centum of the aggregate principal amount of the guaranteed farm improvement loans made by such bank.
In my opinion that guarantee of ten per cent will not produce the result that we have in mind. The guarantee should be higher. I am not sure, but I am of the opinion that in the case of national housing it was at least fifteen per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: It was fifteen per cent on the home improvement loans.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Yes. To make this bill as effective as I hope it will be, I think the guarantee should be twenty per cent rather than ten per cent. If the government guarantee the banks twenty per cent and they charge the creditors four per cent, we may achieve the purpose the government has in mind in this bill. I think these are two important points. I am not satisfied that ten per cent is a sufficient guarantee to make this bill effective.
Section 5 states:
The minister shall not be liable under this act to make any payment to a bank in respect of loss sustained by it as a result of a farm improvement loan made after the aggregate principal amount of guaranteed farm improvement loans made by all banks exceeds two hundred and fifty million dollars or made more than three years after the commencement of this act.
I dealt with that and received answers from the minister yesterday. With regard to the maximum guarantee of S3,000, that is all to the good; but we must bear in mind the fact that when a man applies for this credit he will have to give to the banks the security to which they are entitled. The banks always ask for all the security they can obtain, but it will cut off the applicant's security with other creditors.
Farm Credit-Mr. Cruickshank

In the past two or three years we have had information brought down which proves that under existing conditions it is much more economical to operate a large farm than a small one. Speaking on the budget on March 11 of last year I put on Hansard figures which I had obtained from the officials of the Department of Agriculture, pointing out that at least in the prairie provinces the most economical farm to operate to-day is the two-section farm unit on a diversified basis with certain power equipment. Most of those farmers would be precluded from coming under this measure. Notwithstanding that, I am satisfied that when a man starts to operate on a larger scale it is his duty to make his own financial arrangements, but I do point out that the most efficient operator will not come under this legislation.
Section 6 has to do with regulations. Paragraph (b) of subsection 1 reads as follows: to designate works for the improvement or development of a farm, in addition to those specified in subparagraphs . . .
Then the paragraphs are named. I think this is an important clause, because it will give the government-I presume the minister, or by order in council at least-powers to designate other works. In that connection I want to make a suggestion, namely, that with respect to any works which shall be designated, proper agricultural authorities shall be consulted. I have in mind officers of the federation of agriculture. producers and the officials of producers' organizations. In order to make alterations such as these, to designate other works not provided' for, such officials as the representatives of agricultural producers in this country should be consulted and their advice taken.
Then subsection 2 states:
No regulation shall be effective until published in the Canada Gazette and upon such publication shall be effective and shall have the same force and effect as if it had been enacted in this act.
I think this is rather a new procedure in the last few years. A great deal of this has been done by the wartime prices and trade board officials, and the Minister of Agriculture has taken advantage of this in each of his orders in council in the past few years. I do not think that is good. We should have our statutes and we should put them into effect.
I now come to section 7, which is as follows:
Notwithstanding anything contained in the Bank Act or any other statute, if a bank makes a guaranteed farm improvement loan the principal amount of which exceeds two thousand dollars and the period for repayment of which is longer than five years, the bank may at the time of making the loan take as security for the repayment thereof and the payment of interest thereon-

(a)	a mortgage or hypothec upon the farm
in respect of which the proceds of the loan are to be expended;	.
(b)	an assignment of the rights and interest of a purchaser of the farm under an agreement of sale.
And there is further information in that connection. I think that will prove to any of us who have had experience in these matters that if full advantage is taken of this provision, and I think probably we would take advantage of it if we were in the place of the bankers, practically all the normal credit will be transferred to the banks, and any further credit will be cut off once an applicant comes under this bill. It is important that people should realize this fact. Then section 9, subsection 2, provides:
Any document purporting to be a receipt in the prescribed form and purporting to be signed on behalf of the bank shall :be evidence of the payment by the minister to the bank under this act in respect of the loan therein mentioned and of the execution of such document on behalf of the bank.
This is a phrase which has come into being under our war-time legislation of the past few years, and I think it is a little lax. I would have no fear of what might be done under the present minister, with the present set-up, but I do believe the wording might be tightened up a- little to safeguard the future.
There are four more sections in the bill, with which I do not propose to deal at this time. I would point out to hon. members that the mortgage debt of Canadian agriculture is approximately $700,000,000 to-day, and that this bill provides for a maximum of $250,000,000 or one-third of that total. When you remember that the present mortgage indebtedness will have to be taken into consideration when these people ask for loans under this measure; when you remember that once they come under it further credit will be cut off, I am not so sure that the bill will serve the purpose we have in mind. At the same time I heartily agree with the principle of the measure. I believe it is a step in the right direction, but if it is to be effective it seems to me the government guarantee should be increased to twenty per cent, while the rate of interest should be not more than four per cent. These two changes should be made in order to have this legislation as effective as we would like to see it, in the interests of the average farmer of Canada. I hope these matters will be taken into consideration when the bill is dealt with in the banking and commerce committee.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
I think perhaps I am better fitted to speak on this bill than any other hon. member of the house, because of my long experience with

Farm Credit-Mr. Leader
overdrafts and promissory notes; I am certain my friends in the banks will not dispute my knowledge in that connection. I am going to be very brief; for once I am going to outdo the Progressive Conservatives. I want to support everything that has been said by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), except that I believe four per cent is too high.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: I said not more than four per cent; I believe it should be lower, too.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member agrees with me. It has been admitted by the banking and commerce committee-[DOT] and if they admit anything that is going some -that Canada's greatest hope for the future lies in increased agricultural production, but I do not think we will have that increased production unless money is made more readily available to the primary producers at very low rates of interest. It seems to me that in agriculture, a basic industry, three and a half pier cent is ample; and in addition I believe the minister is killing his own bill when he limits the government's guarantee to ten per cent. Perhaps this is not a popular thing to say politically, but I have never had any difficulty in borrowing money from the banks. Probably what I have borrowed would seem a small amount to the many millionaires in this house, but to me it seemed a great deal. I have not had any difficulty in borrowing it, but I have had a great deal of difficulty in paying it back. As long as I did pay it back, however, I coidd always borrow more. But in limiting the guarantee to ten per cent, I believe the minister is making a mistake.
I agree with the hon. member for Souris that it is very unfair to place this bill in our hands to-day and immediately ask us to put it through. Since I have been in this house I have always heard that agriculture is the most important industry in Canada, yet here we have a bill affecting agriculture which we are asked to endorse or criticize on very short notice indeed. As a matter of fact I have had this bill for exactly five minutes. It seems to me the minister is defeating his own purpose in restricting the guarantee to ten per cent. Any bona fide farmer, as far as I know, would have no difficulty in borrowing to that extent from the chartered banks. As I understand this procedure, the banks lend the money and the dominion guarantee their losses to the extent of ten per cent. Any chartered bank in the beautiful Fraser valley will take the chance of a loss up to ten per cent even now. I would go the hon. member for Souris one better, because our crop is not exactly the same as wheat; I do not think a guarantee of twenty-five per cent would be
too high, and I believe the maximum rate of interest should be three and a half per cent at most.
I am not in a position to go into this bill clause by clause. I agree with everything said by the hon. member for Souris, but I should like to see those two changes made if the bill is to be of any use to the farmers of Fraser valley, the main agricultural district of British Columbia. That is, I should like to see the interest rate reduced and the guarantee increased to at least twenty per cent.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Perhaps a real dirt farmer might be allowed to say a word or two on this bill, though I had not intended to do more than commend the government on at least attempting to make credit available to farmers at low rates of interest, which I believe is the purpose of this legislation.
I agree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank); I do not think anyone has difficulty in borrowing money from the banks provided he has repaid his previous borrowings; and after all I do not think any man, any corporation or any company should borrow from a bank without fully intending to pay back the amount borrowed. A great deal could be said about the high interest rates that farmers have paid in the past. Personally I have paid as high as twelve per cent, and I know of others who up to at least two years ago were paying eight per cent on machinery they had purchased. This bill, I believe, will do away with a great deal of difficulty in that connection.
I do not believe it is a good move to empower the banks to take additional security; I think it will have the effect suggested a moment ago by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). If a farmer gets into difficulties and the bank takes additional security, that farmer will be placed at a disadvantage if he wishes to get any further benefits from the bank or any other institution. However, that is not why I rose. I want to say that I believe the government is wise in restricting its liability to ten per cent, though most of those who have spoken previously have said that this percentage should be increased. The hon. member for Souris would increase it to twenty per cent, and I believe the hon. member for Fraser Valley mentioned twenty-five per cent. I believe that easy credit has ruined more farmers-and I am speaking only for farmers, though perhaps this applies to other trades and professions-than have been put on easy street by bank borrowings. Get the idea into a farmer's mind that he must pay this money
Farm Credit-Mr. Leader

back, and he is going to be very careful when he asks for credit. I think that if the government increases the liability they are going to encourage the banks to be more liberal in their loans. Do not for one moment think that I am condemning the banks for lending money to needy borrowers. That is not my intention at all. The point I make is that easy credit is going to ruin many men. And if the banks accept a liability higher than ten per cent it will mean easy credit for many of our farmers.
The other point I make is one where I take issue with the hon. member for Souris-and I have had to do so on several occasions. However I think I know whereof I speak. I have heard men declare-not farmers, so often, but. the men who farm the farmers, as we have heard it said-that it is more economical to grow wheat on a large farm than to grow it on smaller farms. I will not agree with that. And when the hon. member for Souris says that a two-section farmer is the economic unit, I disagree with him entirely, I think that that is the class of farmer that got us into trouble with our big wheat surplus-a condition we have now overcome because of the war. In my opinion the economic unit is the smaller farmer on the half section or three-quarter section of land. He may have three or four sons, and in that event could probably have a section. The men on those smaller farms are diversified in their farming operations, and do not depend entirely upon the growing of wheat and other grains. They do not build up big surpluses to depress the prices for the smaller farmers.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: I referred to a diversified farm.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Well, some might call two sections of land a diversified farm. But the smaller farmer must practice diversification, because he cannot put all his eggs in one basket. He has to keep live stock, and that live stock will build up any farm, whether it be one of 2,000 acres or only a quarter section. I know that the farmers who stood the stress of the years of depression were the smaller farmers. You can find that in every province of Canada. And when we are encouraged to build up larger farms, or what are called more economic units, I believe we are making a mistake. What do we want? With less than one-third of Canadians living on the farms in Canada to-day, what we want is more farmers on the land. The 2,000-acre farmer is perhaps living in a city or town, and has his farm operated by a hired man who runs one or two tractors. Get the farmers out on the smaller farms. Build the country in that way, and we
{Mr. Leader.]
will build from a proper foundation, not only in Canada but, I believe, throughout the world.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, farmers are always thankful for small mercies, and I think they will appreciate a rate of interest of five per cent, particularly if they had to start out, as I did, by borrowing at eight per cent. And that eight per cent was compounded every three months. If they had crop failures for four years in succession, as I had when I started out, then I think they will appreciate this rate all the more. I know my interest bills, like those of many others, had piled up so high I was not able to stand them.
The fact that this money is being made available will help out, provided that other steps are taken as well. I am thinking particularly of the mention made yesterday of the prices of farm machinery-and what I have to say about farm machinery will apply with equal force to a number of other products. I believe it was in 1936 and 1937 that the committee on agriculture investigated farm machinery prices. In one instance the committee found that one implement company was following up the practice now followed by the banks, that of having a secret reserve. In that instance it was one of $40,000,000, -which had been piled up from excess profits they were receiving. I do not know whether the other implement companies did the same thing, but at least one company under investigation was found to have a secret reserve of the amount I have mentioned. Those prices will have to be investigated, and they will have to be placed upon a sounder basis. If purchases are made for cash it is only reasonable to expect that the prices charged to-day might well be considerably reduced.
This programme would also relieve unemployment. It took the present war to relieve the unemployment of 1939. What I have suggested would also provide an outlet for the factories located in central Canada. Before going further I would point out to the minister that he is starting entirely at the wrong end. If a person has a sore on his hand or on his face he may put salve on it, but he will find that that will not do much good. He must go to the root of the trouble. Remove the cause and the sore will usually take care of itself.
For the information of the minister-and I assume he knows this already-I should like to place on record the percentages of national income received by agriculture over a period of years. I do this because about one-third of our population is engaged in that industry. I do it, too, because the workers in agriculture work from one and a half to twice as many hours as do those engaged in other industries. For these reasons I feel satisfied we should

Farm Credit-Mr. Fair
receive at least one-third of the national income. Beginning with the year 1926 the following are the percentages of national income received by the agricultural population:
Percentage of
Year	national income
1926		 17-8
1927		 10-4
1928		 17-6
1929		 14-6
1930		 9-6
1931		 6-3
1932		 5-0
1933		 6-6
1934		 9-1
1935		 9-3
1936		 11-4
1937		 11-5
1938		 10-9
1939		 12-5
1940		 11-0
It will be noted that in that wonderful depression year, 1932, the farmers of Canada, comprising one-third of our population, received only five per cent of the national income. These percentages work out to an average of 11-3 per cent over the fifteen-year period. Instead of extending this credit to farmers, some action should be taken to give them the percentage of the national income to which they are entitled. If that were done the necessity for this bill would be eliminated. I am not saying the bill should not be put into effect, for the time being. But I do say that even at the expense of those who are farming the farmers and profiteering to an abnormal extent to-day, steps should be taken immediately to place agriculture on a sound footing, for the first time since Canada was Canada.
I am, of course, in favour of the bill. I may have something further to say later on, but I would repeat, for the benefit of the minister and his colleagues, that until agriculture is placed upon a sound .footing we are going to have an unending succession of farm debts.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been said, this bill has been in our hands only since this morning. Since receiving it I have been trying to ascertain whether an irrigation farm may benefit under it. It is not clear to me, and I should like the minister to explain whether it does or does not. Section 2, paragraph (h), subparagraph (v), refers to the erection or construction of works for drainage on a farm, but there is no reference to machinery or equipment such as would be used on an irrigated farm. Section 6, regulations, states:
The governor in council may, on the recommendation of the minister, make regulations:
(a) to define for the purposes of this act the following expressions:
(ii) "works for drainage".
A considerable amount of farming in Canada is carried on under irrigation, and there are signs that this will be increased in the near future. It is a common thing for the farmer growing crops under irrigation to require assistance to purchase pumping machinery and various items of equipment required for the carriage of water to his land. When the minister replies I should like him to be good enough to say whether or not such requirements will be included in the clauses of this bill.
Hon. VV. E. ROWE (Dufferin-Simcoe): Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) has said, this bill has not been very long in our hands and it is difficult to discuss it on such short notice. However, the need for the bill may be defined in many ways. The previous speaker referred to the disparity in the prices of farm products and other things. That is one of the basic reasons, [DOT] not only for the depression in agriculture but for unemployment generally in this country, and it no doubt creates one of the needs for farm credit. However, I believe that even over and above that one of the needs for this bill has been created by the fact that we have farm loan boards in the different provinces; we have the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which was passed by the dominion, and we have other efforts being made to extend credit to the country but not serving the purpose for which they were initiated. I fear that with this bill we are going to create further embarrassment for the farmer who wants to borrow money. If parliament sanctions a bill which goes so far in granting credit to farmers and then fails to go far enough to make it practicable, it is obvious to all of us who have had experience with farm loans, who have had experience in agriculture enterprises generally, that there are grave dangers hidden behind the inadequacy of the bill.
I believe it was the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) who said that ten per cent was not sufficient. I find myself in full agreement with that. I believe the farmer should have his loan at four per cent if possible, and I hope there will be an amendment to that effect. If that is done, I doubt whether the ten per cent risk guaranteed by the government will make these loans sufficiently attractive to the local bank managers to make them want to extend the credit required.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), who preceded me, stated that easy credit is not sound credit. There is no one in business and I doubt if there is any one in this house, who does not realize the
Farm Credit-Mr. Rowe

dangers of easy credit for the young or the old, for the business man or the farmer. We all know it is sometimes ruinous, and to that extent I agree with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. But I think he will agree with me, and I believe you will also, sir, when I say that there is a need for essential credit. There is a difference between easy credit and hard credit and essential credit.
We are living to-day in an age of advancement. I realize the good motives behind the statement of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie when he said that what we need are small farms, such as fruit farms, poultry farms and mixed farms. As the hon. member knows, for many years in this house I have urged the diversification of agriculture. He will recall that I twitted the western farmers for developing a lopsided agriculture. However, I have been in this house long enough to see the western farmer become almost as diversified in his production as the farmer in the east. The only difference is that he is farming larger units.
Progress knows no retreat. You cannot stop advancement. There is no enterprise in this dominion which offers greater possibilities for research in the use of modem equipment and advancement in general than agriculture. I have farmed all my life, and my forefathers before me. I will admit that I do not know all about agriculture. I have heard some speakers in this house who knew more than I, but I have heard one or two speakers who I am convinced knew less. With all respect to those who have the same motives as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, may I say that after this war is over I would like to see happy families on small farms, but I would hate to see a bill that retarded the general progress of agriculture itself.
I have farmed on reasonably sized farms. My main experience has been with farms of around four hundred acres, but I have had experience on farms ranging from one hundred acres up to four hundred. Some of the smaller farms have done better than mine, but just as many of the larger farms have done better. I am convinced that with the march of progress that is obvious to us all, with the modern machinery that will come out following this war, no matter how desirable it may be to have small farms with the old team and the single furrow plough, the small cultivator and the-

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Race horses.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Some race horses add a little bit of mirth to a class which is just as much entitled to it as any other class in this dominion. When you have the experience of seeing a boy of twelve or fourteen years go

out and plough more in one day than three hired men can with high-class teams of horses in a full week, you begin to count the cost. You then realize that you cannot stop progressive development. It is not easy credit; it is essential credit.
While it is true that the man on the small farm may not need more than the limit of $3,000 provided in paragraph (d) of subsection (1) of section (3); while he may not need $2,000 or perhaps no more than $700, in progressive times like these a limit of $3,000 is pretty small for the large farm. My hon. friends may say that in general that is enough, but there is something I want to place before hon. members who I know are just as much interested as I in this great industry. Once you have a credit of x dollars as the limit, you automatically destroy the chances of the farmer getting a loan anywhere else. I well recall that the government which I was supporting brought in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I discussed it at great length privately with the government of the day and also in the house. That act may have helped in some respects.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Of course it did.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: My hon. friend says it did, but it was the general opinion of farmers throughout Ontario that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act seriously injured the credit of the farmers of Ontario. The old retired farmer or the lawyer ini the village who was handling a widow's estate and had money to lend would say to an applicant, a voung couple perhaps who came in for a loan of $2,000 to buy a $10,000 farm, "No, I am sorry, George, I cannot lend you the money because I got a trimming under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act."

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Don't call him
George.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Fraser Valley looks so prosperous that I do not think he would ever need credit, and if he did, I am sure he could get it without any trouble. I have had scores of men come and ask me where I thought they could borrow money. I have sent them to the old line creditors, perhaps a retired farmer or a lawyer handling a widow's estate, and they would come back to me afterwards and say that they were refused the loan because the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act had frightened creditors off. We have had a farm loan act in Ontario and money was not being lent under that act for a good part of the time; I say that without reflecting on any government. At times the government was collecting more than it

Farm Credit-Mr. Rowe
was lending under the act, and I believe that that is the case to-day. I am not saying that from any political point of view. I merely wish to emphasize the fact that because that act was on the statute book it frightened the normal creditor away.
Mr. ILSLEY. I do not see that at all.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: I do not believe it.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
I have seen it; I believe it; I have felt it; I have evidence of it. There is not a member from Ontario who does not know that that is so. If the minister sets up a farm loan agency under this act, he is going into the field of lending money to the farmer, and if the farmer cannot get enough money from him and applies to somebody else, he will be met with the reply, "The government has a lending agency, and if you cannot get the money there, do not expect me to take your risk."
I submit therefore that the bank must be in a position to consider freely the risk it is asked to carry, and it must be in a position to be reasonably lenient to the farmer, because almost every other line of credit will have been eliminated. I say this in fairness to our local bankers. The local bank manager is usually a good citizen. I do not believe he is going to take an undue risk even with the government taking twenty per cent of the loss, but he will be more sympathetic and will feel freer to sit down in his office with the farmer who needs a loan, knowing that twenty per cent of any loss is guaranteed by the government. But if the local banker under these circumstances is not sympathetic and refuses the man a loan, where else can he get credit? The old retired farmer who might have lent him money will say, "Have you been to your bank and borrowed money under this new act?" and if the man says, "Yes, but the fellow down at the bank was never friendly to me and he will not let me have the money," the retired farmer will say, "Have you any implements?" I am simply bringing out the point that if the local banker does not give the borrower a sympathetic hearing, he has nobody else in the village to whom he can go to borrow money.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, my understanding is that this is not to take the place of mortgages but is providing for loans to enable agriculture to carry on.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: I was just coming to that. It guarantees the bank ten per cent of its loss on loans on improvements and implements.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
To enable the
farmer to carry on.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Yes, to carry on. Section
3(1)(d) says:
the principal amount of the loan did not at the time of the making of the loan, together with the amount owing in respect of other farm improvement loans previously made to the borrower and disclosed in his application, or of which the bank had knowledge, exceed the sum of three thousand dollars.
Another section of the bill provides that the bank may take a farm mortgage up to $3,000, and I was just coming to that feature.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Only if the loan exceeds $2,000 and the period for repayment is longer than five years.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Yes. I come to the other angle, in reply to the hon. member for Fraser Valley. Under this bill you are in almost the same lending field on mortgages as you are on loans. A loan of $3,000 may be sufficient for the small farmer, but $3,000 is not a very big loan to a farmer who is farming with mechanical equipment. But when you have a mortgage on his land he cannot get credit anywhere else, no matter how big his farm may be.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Would not that man utilize the Canadian farm loan board for a longer term loan, which would not affect his credit to the same extent?

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: I agree. The Canadian farm loan board takes mortgages not only on the ground but on the chattels. You have already used the mortgage on the chattels. On the other hand, if the farm loan board can take mortgages, why put mortgages in this bill at all?

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Just for special cases.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
That is the very point I am endeavouring to make. I want the minister to think this over seriously. We should not touch the loan field in any one of these cases unless we can go as far as it is economically sound to go, because, whatever field you touch, for that particular field you will detract from the attraction of the ordinary normal creditor. Personally I would rather see this bill go through the house guaranteeing twenty per cent instead of ten per cent. I hope it is possible. I realize that there are many difficulties. I hope it is possible to make loans at four per cent; I think it is desirable; and the banks could be assured of twenty per cent. I say this in all seriousness. To my mind there is little more risk being taken. Your bank managers are sound business men, and can help the farmers and business people generally across the dominion by sound advice. I am not so sure that if you gave them sufficient backing you would not get the best pro-
Farm Credit-Mr. Rowe

tection for the treasury and the dominion that could possibly be secured in Canada. But give them sufficient backing, or support, or guarantee, whichever term you choose to use, to enable them at least to function. If you do, they will be more apt to deal sympathetically with the farmers' requirements.
So far as the farm mortgage part of it is concerned, I think that should be eliminated. Either eliminate it or leave it to the discretion of the banker to fix a higher limit. In other words, you should not enter that field at all to disturb the possibilities of the farmer getting the loan from the farm loan board.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
What does the
hon. member mean by a higher limit-ten per cent, or twenty per cent, or what?

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: A higher guarantee. It should not be restricted to $3,000. I realize that our farm land prices, especially in Ontario, through the years of depression from 1930 to 1940 have gone to a pretty low level at times, but I am convinced that there were literally scores of farms that would have been sold and sold at reasonably good prices and young men would have started on them had they been able to find credit. In ninety per cent of these cases, in the province of Ontario, the reason why they could not find credit was that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act frightened the old line lenders.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
I do not want to
interrupt the hon. member. He states that in ninety per cent of the cases he mentions the reason why loans could not be secured was that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act frightened lenders. Will he not agree that the reason was in large part the fact that the economic situation was such that the prices of agricultural products were too low?

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
That is quite true, and I
thought I said that at the outset. But I am speaking of Ontario. Let me put it this way. Ninety per cent of the old normal type of creditor, the retired farmer or the lawyer who had money in trust, were eliminated because the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act ruined credit. I do not think this will ruin credit, but it will restrict the extension of credit and take it out of that field.
I would urge the minister therefore to reconsider first the ten per cent guarantee and make it twenty per cent. I would ask him to reconsider the mortgage clause and either make it adequate so that it will work in practice, or eliminate it so that it will not be required, and allow the farm loan board or other mortgage agencies to deal with mortgages as required. I would much prefer a mortgage of 810,000 on some farms to a mort-

gage of $3,000 on some other farms. It depends on the ratio. It is better for the government to extend through their bank a mortgage of $10,000 on a $15,000 farm than a mortgage of $3,000 on a $4,000 farm, and I see no reason why it should be fixed at any particular figure. Certainly if it is fixed at a figure, that figure should not be the arbitrary amount of $3,000, because in my opinion that would be only a nuisance mortgage.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Would you not put on any limit at all?

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: There is no limit except ten per cent; you can get all you want.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
A limit of $2,000 or $3,000 on implements, or to assist in improvements, might well stay at that level. Even $3,000 is not a reckless risk to take in connection with general equipment required on the average successful farm, where that includes live stock and farm implements. But when you go into the other field you find that the amount proposed is too small. It is too small to assist and therefore becomes a nuisance mortgage. And it is the first mortgage. I would like to know if there is any member in this house who would find anyone to take a second mortgage under these circumstances when it is so difficult to get the first.
I suggest therefore that the minister consider either the elimination of the mortgage clause or the desirability of making it sufficiently flexible to enable it to work. I am convinced that there is not a single feature that will endanger the credit of farmers more than allowing the government to take the first mortgage and leaving it to doubtful lenders to take the second.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Under this act it is not
necessarily the first.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: It may not necessarily be the first, according to the letter-

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Would they take a second?

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
That is the question. I say
to the minister:	Is it going to be your
practice to take a second?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
The government is not going to operate it. The government will be supervising it, but not operating it. The banks will operate it.
v Mr. CRUICKSHANK:	Will the banks
take a second?

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
They will never take a
second.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
With the government supervising and the bank operating it, and knowing

Farm Credit-Mr. Hansell
the present Minister of Finance, as I know him, and it is only to his credit to say so,
I am sure he will be very leery about a second one. Even he, in all his kindness, will leave it to John Jones, the retired farmer in the district, and John Jones will shake his head, as an hon. member over there is doing, and will decline to touch it. The farmer will then go to the farm loan board and someone will come and examine his farm. He will then say to the farmer, "You went to the bank, did you not?" The farmer will say "Yes." Then the other will say to the farmer, "You could not get it from the dominion?" "No." Well, whether it might be politic or not, the other man will say to the farmer, "You could not get credit from the government, and there must be some reason for that, because they can throw billions around here and there; they are not so small in their loans. If your credit were good they would have given it to you."
I am not critical of the bill, but I am throwing this out as a warning. I know the purpose is to help the farmer with reasonable credit rather than to injure him, but I fear that the purpose in view will not be achieved, and in the end, crude as this may sound, despite our good intentions, we may simply be adding insult to injury and depriving the farmer of other credit which he might have been able to obtain.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: In discussing this bill providing short term credits to farmers for the improvement of their farms I do not do so as an agricultural expert. I -will admit, of course, that I know very little about farming and agriculture in general. I might dip one of my hands in one sack of wheat and the other in another and compare the two, and I would not know that there was very much difference, except that one might look a little bigger than the other.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: They may both be oats.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
They may be something else. I may look at two cows and I think I would know the difference between a Holstein and a Jersey. Once upon a time I did see a picture of the leader of the Progressive Conservative party milking a cow; I knew then which was the cow, but I do not claim to be an agricultural expert. I do not think it requires an abundance of knowledge about agriculture to discuss this bill. I do not knowhow much the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsleyl knows about agriculture, but I do know that he knows something about finance, about banking, about credit institutions, about mortgages and related subjects, and he is the
man who brings down the bill. It is purely a bill which concerns those who are interested in monetary affairs.
I do not think we can very well oppose the measure, because after all Canada's orthodox Minister of Finance is bringing it in for the purpose of helping the farmer to get credit on easier terms. While we may support the bill, what is actually needed is more fundamental legislation, legislation that would have the effect of putting the farmer m such a position that he would not have to borrow money for the improvement of property, buying machinery and things in general on his farm. Of course I am not saying that industry ever operates without certain credit facilities; whether it is secondary industry or primary industry they all find it necessary to borrow money, pay overdrafts, and so on. But I do say that what is needed is some legislation that would fundamentally change the present system of financial operations. When that is done, agriculture will have its chance, and secondary industry, though a bit better off in past years than agriculture, will also be in a better position. The fact of the matter is that fundamentally industry is never self-liquidating under the present system of borrowing.
This bill is a measure to provide loans for improvement of farms. Anything that will improve the farm will make it more valuable.
I agree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) when he says that the difficulty is not borrowing money but being able to pay it back. The difference between agriculture and secondary industry is that when secondary industry borrows money for the purpose of production those borrowings are written into the costs of its production. The result is that when the goods are sold the loans are retrieved and paid back. But that is not what happens with agriculture. The main difference is that secondary industry puts a price tag on its production that meets the requirements of the debt, but the farmer never puts a price tag on his production. He is a gambler-not that he wants to be, but the very nature of his business makes him one. He has to accept the available price for his production and take a chance on whether or not that available price will enable him to retire his debt.
I should like to see a crop failure paragraph in this bill, because the farmer operates on a yearly basis. If he has a crop failure one year his loan is still held intact, and he finds it necessary to continue to pay the interest on that loan-

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Compounded.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
As my hon. friend says, compounded. That happens whether he has
Farm Credit-Mr. Hansell

a crop failure or not. The fact of the matter is it does not cost the bank anything to carry that loan for another year. That may be subject to a lot of discussion. As a matter of fact the banks do not lend the farmer anything, in reality. The banks lend debt. When the farmer goes to the bank he gets a debt in the form of financial figures. The only obligation that is imposed upon the banks-and I am using a crop failure year as an illustration -is what it costs to carry that debt, which is very little. When I say, "costs to carry the debt" I suppose I shall have to include the interest of one and a half per cent that the banks have to pay when that debt becomes deposits in the savings accounts of the people. Therefore I say there should be a debt paragraph in the bill which in a crop failure year would stay the increase of the debt in so far as interest is concerned. There would be no interest in a crop failure year.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has told us of the danger to farmers by reason of their being able 'to obtain easy credit. I may agree with him there, but I would also say that any credit is a danger, whether it be easy credit or hard credit. Any credit is a danger because credit given to farmers by banks is a debt, and any credit is a danger in that sense. There is only one credit that is not a danger, and that is social credit.
I wonder if the minister, in discussing this bill, took the various agricultural organizations into his confidence. I do not know that it would help him very much, I must confess, because in reading much that is published by agricultural organizations I notice that they tackle almost every farm problem except the problem of farm debt. They deal with almost everything affecting agriculture, including markets, but somehow or other they do not seem to deal with the problem of a proper fiscal policy for the farmer. They may think they do, but I must confess that I find a sad lack in their literature in this regard. For instance, may I quote from a pamphlet issued by the Canadian federation of agriculture, which is rather enlightening. This is an address which was broadcast by Mr. Pearson, who is our representative on the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, with respect to the Hot Springs conference. I heard the broadcast, and thought it was very good. This statement is very significant:
The application of science to agriculture has for the first time in history now given man the physical means for conquering want. Whether he has the economic sense and the social wisdom so to apply his scientific and productive knowledge that the food which is grown gets to all the people-well, that is another question.
[Mr. HanseU.i
That is the question, and Mr. Pearson does not go into the problem of how the food is to be distributed to the world, which I claim is a fundamental difficulty that has to be solved. If it is a matter of distribution, then it is a question of money. Then I have an address by Mr. Paul Appleby, which is also issued by the Canadian federation of agriculture. In these remarks I am not criticizing the federation; I am simply suggesting that while they have attempted to solve many problems of agriculture they do not seem to have tackled the most fundamental problem of all. I have mentioned this address by Mr. Appleby; I do not find any of my markings in this pamphlet, so I fancy I need not comment on that. In any case these people will know that I read their literature. Another publication by the federation is entitled " Farmers Meet the Cabinet," and it is very interesting. I do not know whether they got very far, but the pamphlet contains a paragraph on government subsidies. I am not going to read it, because I do not want to take the time of the house in doing so, but it gives the psychological impression that they are more or less apologizing because the government have given subsidies to agriculture, and they argue that after all the subsidy is given to benefit the consumer. That argument is right; I have no quarrel with it, but let me say that agriculture has no reason whatever to apologize for government subsidies. I agree with them, and I have no particular criticism to offer of the financial policy of the government in respect to subsidies. I do say, however, that agriculture is not self-liquidating under the present debt-creating system. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) said he wanted agriculture put on a proper footing. So do I; so do we all. We want agriculture in such a position that with parity prices it will be able to pay its way. But let me add that in my humble opinion if one branch of Canadian industry is self-liquidating, it is at the expense of another branch of Canadian industry almost going into bankruptcy.
I am not going to say anything more about this matter of government subsidies, Mr. Speaker, because I am afraid you are apt to say it is a bit out of order, though as a matter of fact when we come to discuss a bill of this kind we are almost bound to discuss the operation of agriculture in respect to prices. Now I have another pamphlet issued by the Canadian federation of agriculture which deals with the federation itself; what it is, how it works and what it advocates. On page 11 they talk about farm income, and the concluding paragraph reads:
The federation believes that until the principle is accepted that farmers are entitled to

Farm Credit-Mr. Neill
a fair exchange value for the products of the farm with the products and services of nonfarm groups, there can be no secure future for agriculture.
In reality all that is said in this paragraph is that there must be parity prices; but if I am correct in saying that industry is not self-liquidating under a debLcreating system, parity prices of themselves will not do the trick for agriculture. I should point out, however, that on page 14 of this pamphlet I find one short paragraph dealing with farm credit. I do not think I need read it, for it simply says that farm credit should be available. With all that, however, they do not seem to recognize what is inherently the fundamental problem of all industry.
I shall close, Mr. Speaker, simply by saying that it seems to me such an organization as tlie Canadian federation of agriculture should have within itself a body or a committee of economic advisers. And may I suggest that if they ever have such a committee, it is of no use to have economic advisers who have not been able to advise in days gone by. They must be economic advisers with a new idea, advisers who know what is wrong and who will advise as to the right way out.
As I have said, I am going to support the bill. It is purely and simply an orthodox bill. It will not do the trick; do not think it will. It will not save the farmer completely; it will help to lengthen his suffering days, but just the same I will vote for it.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
I think the general opinion of hon. members is that this is a good bill. Any criticism that has been offered has been in an endeavour to make the legislation more useful, and has consisted of two suggestions; first, that the rate of interest should be reduced, and second that the government's share of responsibility should be greater. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Eowe) introduced a new angle along this line. He pointed out something which is no doubt correct-although I do not give it the emphasis that he did- that under this bill it might be possible for a bank to take a mortgage for a small loan. They have that power under the act. That would to a large extent cut off a man's credit. He would not be able to get credit otherwise, once it was discovered that the bank had a mortgage on his property, even for a small amount.
However I do not anticipate the trouble anticipated by the hon. member, and for two reasons. The first is that this is primarily intended to be a small loan bill to help farmers in a small way and, as I understand it, for a comparatively temporary period. The
purpose of the bill is not to finance a farmer, but rather to help him. And unless a farmer has some stake in his land, and some reasonable assets, it is not proposed that this bill will enable him to start farming and finance him for his land, implements, stock and everything else. This is regarded more as a temporary matter.
On the other hand there is this feature, that even if he had a small loan for two or three hundred dollars, if he afterwards deemed it advisable to get a larger loan he could always get it under the Canadian Farm Loan Act, and he could repay this temporary loan.
I agree with those who have advocated that the rate of interest should be reduced. That would only bring it in line with the interest charged under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I have had long experience with farmers, and I know that the less mortgage a farmer has, the better. He cannot afford to pay the high rate of interest which perhaps it would be fair enough to charge those engaged in some other lines of activity. If he is going to have any mortgage, then he should be able to get it at a low rate of interest. In my view four per cent, or even three and a half per cent, would be reasonable.
That, of course, would require consideration of the other objection which has been raised, namely, that the government should take a larger share of the loss, if any. It has been suggested that it be raised from ten per cent to twenty per cent. This would be essential if the lower rate of interest is conceded. Because even at five per cent I doubt if the average bank would be bothered. They are getting only a ten per cent repayment from the government, and their loans would be small. They can lend money at as much as six or eight per cent, and they are not going to be bothered with it. You can lead a horse to water but you cannot make him drink. And our appeal will not make them lend money if the proposal is not a reasonable one. Therefore, if we are to compel them to lend at four per cent it would be reasonable to expect the government to assume a greater responsibility of the ultimate loss, if any.
One other point, and it is this. According to the bill the governor in council may make regulations dealing with so many different matters that they extend over a page and a half. Well, I suppose that is necessary, but it entails great danger. For heaven's sake let the government use its power to make these regulations as simple as possible, and make the process of getting loans under this measure as rapid as possible. The government passed a reasonably simple act in respect of old age
Farm Credit-Mr. Neill

pensions, and gave power to somebody to make regulations. Those regulations made a completely new bill; one would hardly recognize it as the same bill. I hope the government will exercise its control in the present instance and prevent anything of that kind- because it is quite possible to condemn the bill entirely by way of regulations. They can go all over the shop with these regulations, and if that is done inadvisedly it will mean that the bill would be of no use at all.
Following out that idea I would impress upon the government the fact that a great deal of the advantage in connection with loans of this kind is that a man can get a loan quickly. If he cannot get it quickly it is not worth much to him. There may be an auction sale, or a man may have a chance to buy sheep at a low price. If he can get money in a few hours or in a few days, well and good. If not, a provision of this kind is of very little use to him.
A few years ago a man came to my office wanting to borrow $200. I told him all about the Canadian Farm Loan Act, and about the procedure he would have to follow. "But", he said, "I want the money now. I do not want to wait three or four weeks, or perhaps six weeks, while they go all through the red tape three thousand miles away. I want the money now." It was of no use to him if he could not get it right away. Instead of borrowing from the government at four per cent or five per cent I lent him the money at six per cent, and he later repaid it. The point I make is that he was willing to pay six or eight per cent to get quick action. That is the main thing in connection with these small loans, when a man goes to buy a bull, a horse or something of the kind. The regulations may say, "You have to write to Jones." Then Jones sends you a form. You fill out the form, and you sign your name. Then in the fulness of time you are advised that you have misspelt a word and you have to begin again. Then it is sent to Ottawa, and the man at Ottawa is on holidays -and I have seen this happen-and the usefulness of the loan has passed.
This is a good bill, and a good principle, but it should be made as simple as possible and the interest rate should be cut down. Make it worth the bank's while. I am not advocating the interests of the bank-it is most unpopular to defend the banks these days; one would think they were the spawn of the devil. But we cannot compel the banks to lend money, and if we do not give them a reasonable deal they will not be bothered. Therefore my suggestion would be to reduce the interest rate and make the regulations simple.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I object to the second reading of the bill this afternoon. We received a copy of it as late as eleven o'clock this morning, and have had only two or three hours to look over it. I suggest to you that members did not have enough time to digest the contents of the bill or to analyse what it contains. Therefore they are not in a position to discuss intelligently an important measure of this kind.
I do not wish to reflect upon those who have already spoken, but I say that any measure affecting approximately a third of our population should be printed a few days before it is debated in the house, and should be distributed to members of parliament so that they may be in a position to give it study before being asked to comment upon its merits or demerits. This measure will affect approximately thirty per cent of the people in this country. Agriculture has been our fundamental industry, and upon its success depends the success of people in many walks of life. I agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) when he says that agricultural organizations should have been consulted. In my opinion the bill'should have been printed a few days ago and distributed both to agricultural organizations and to members of parliament, so that they might be properly prepared to make their comments.
Divorce bills are usually printed well in advance, bills which most of us hardly read, but a measure of this sort is rushed through as quickly as possible and we have little or no time to look it over.
I would draw your attention to section 7, special powers of bank, which reads:
-if a bank makes a guaranteed farm improvement loan the principal amount of which exceeds two thousand dollars and the period for repayment of which is longer than five years, the bank may at the time of making the loan take as security for the repayment thereof and the payment of interest thereon-
(b) an assignment of the rights and interest of a purchaser of the farm under an agreement of sale.
To me this section indicates that if a bank takes a mortgage upon a farm home and the farmer fails to meet his debt on time, he will be forced to give up his land. In 1938 the province of Alberta passed the home owners' security act which was later disallowed by this government. The purpose of that act was to prohibit the foreclosure or sale under mortgage of any farm home. I suggest that ten years from now many of our western Canadian farmers will find themselves in a position similar to the one they were in from 1929 to 1939 and the financial institutions will proceed to foreclose upon their homes.

Farm Credit-Mr. Iilynka
I intend to support the bill, but object strongly to any provision which would permit a lending institution to foreclose upon the home of a citizen of this country. The family is an important institution in our nation, and we must have high regard for its welfare. Every family should have a home. If a mortgage is given upon land by a farmer I say that the home of the family should not be allowed to be sold for a debt. The time will come when the farmers of this nation will demand from the government that such a bill be passed so that they may be sure that at least they will have a home from which no one can evict them.
I notice that the bill provides for a total of not more than $250,000,000 in loans over a period of years. At the end of 1941 the private debts of our Canadian farmers amounted to $629,000,000, which works out to $2,372 per farm. The $250,000,000 provided in this bill is only a fraction of the money which the farmers of this nation owe to-day. and that does not include the debt written off and other private debts not covered by mortgages.
On a previous occasion I gave the house the details of the indebtedness as it stood in 1941 and as it affected the farmers in each province. I do not intend to repeat the remarks I made previously, except to say that forty-eight per cent of all owned farms in Canada are mortgaged. To me that is an indication that there must be something very much wrong. I have just received a pamphlet from the national farm radio forum and it has this to say under the heading of "The Federal Intermediate Credit Banks":
The present rate in effect in the continental United States is one and a half per cent and in Puerto Rico two per cent.
Why is it not possible for Canadian banks to make credit available to our farmers at one and a half or two per cent interest? The hon. member for Comox-Alberni referred to the fact that we shall be providing credit to our returned men at three and a half per cent. Why should we not be able to provide our farmers with lower rates of interest?
The government promises to guarantee certain losses up to ten per cent. I do not know that I can say much about that at this time. May I say, however, that no matter how honest and efficient a farmer may be, if he is forced to sell his production at below the cost of production, if he is not given protection from the hazards of nature, he will fail to meet his debt obligations. This has been proved by the experience of the past, particularly in the period from 1929 to 1939. The farmer must get parity prices for his products, and not on the 1926-29 level which is used by the Minister of Agriculture.
It should be a parity price which will constitute a proper relationship between the prices which the farmer gets for his products and the prices which he has to pay for the goods he buys. Again, the farmer must be protected from the losses caused by hail and frost and other hazards of nature so that he may be in a position to meet his debt obligations as they fall due.
The minister knows very well that the government has no say as to the amount of credit in circulation, and as this power rests in the hands of the banks, I suggest to him that the banks will restrict credit in the future and then proceed to foreclose on the homes of the farmers. I wish to underline the necessity of amending section 7 (1) (b) and so give protection to the banks in lending to the farmer and at the same time protect the home of the farmer from foreclosure.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) condemn this measure I am surprised that he stated earlier in his remarks that he would support it.
I think we sometimes overlook just what the purpose of this bill is. It is not designed to take away or remove entirely the facilities that now exist for people securing credit from other sources. For instance, the farmer who has victory bonds, as no doubt many of them now have, would have one of the best sources of security with which to go to a bank and borrow money, and he would be able to borrow it at a lower rate than is proposed in this measure. This legislation to me is merely a step in advance of what we already have. It is to meet the particular requirements of a class who have perhaps experienced some difficulty in the past in securing the credit which they need. We have had in existence the Canadian farm loan board which provides for a particular type of long term credit. We have, in addition, banks and private individuals lending for other purposes. The type of loan provided for by this measure fits in between these two- other types of loans, and the bill is designed, as I see it, to meet a little more than 'the ordinary seasonal requirements of farmers, and to take care of requirements that continue beyond one season into another.
Let me illustrate by taking the case of a man who wants to buy a farm implement and has not sufficient money to pay for it in cash. Heretofore we all know that the farm implement companies have provided a good deal of the credit facilities for that type of business. They have naturally been obliged to protect themselves by perhaps adding to their prices and by securing a rate of interest sufficient to cover that type of business. I
Farm Credit-Mr. Weir

look upon this measure as designed to meet that type of requirement, so that a man who wants to buy some farm implement will be able to go to the bank and secure a loan, giving security on the implement he is about to buy, and receiving a loan at a rate of 5 per cent, enabling him to make a cash deal with the implement company.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) appeared to be afraid that the entry of the government into this field of lending might have the effect of drying up other sources of credit. I do not think his fears in that regard are well founded. I think that other sources of credit have been affected for reasons other than government lending. Governments have come into the picture and have provided credit, it is true, and in the matter of farm mortgage loans, particularly in western Canada at the present time, it can be assumed that the government agency is making most of the loans and that private loans have largely dried up. That is to be regretted, and I agree with the hon. member to that extent; but other conditions have been partly responsible -for that. The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, as the hon. member suggested, has undoubtedly played a part as well in drying up other sources of credit. Other forms of security have taken a prior position to the farm mortgage as first-class security, but the same credit facilities will still be available for the man whose assets make him in the eyes of the bank a creditworthy risk. That is all I want to say with respect to that particular feature.
I wish to draw the minister's attention to the banking facilities that are available in most parts of western Canada. I look at the area around Winnipeg. The banks are naturally located there and they do a considerable country business. There is not a rural bank in the area with which I am familiar within forty or fifty miles of Winnipeg. This is the point which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) made, that the banks are not conveniently located to meet the needs of those requiring this type of loan.
There is another thing I have in mind in regard to this measure as it will be operated by the banks. I am not suggesting that it should be handled by any other means, but city banks, for example, are managed largely by the city type of banker, not by a rural banker, and I am just wondering if that type of banker would give the same attention to farm loan requirements that the experienced country banker would. I- have all kinds of confidence in the country type of banker so far as the requirements of the farmer are concerned, but since our country banking facilities are very limited, full account should be taken

of this aspect of the matter. If the city banker does not like doing farm business, the position of the farmer in getting accommodation under this legislation is going to be weakened. I shall be obliged if the minister when he is making his reply to the observations that have been made this afternoon will make some comment on that.

Nevertheless I am going to express my opinion on this measure. As I understand the bill before the house, it is merely a repetition of the Industrial Development bank bill applied to agriculture and my hope is that the banking and commerce committee will have sufiicient sense to consider carefully the whole matter of banks as they now exist and will refrain from recommending any extension of bank charters, from making any decision on the extension of charters, on the industrial development bank, or with regard to farmer's intermediate and short term credit, or the Quebec savings banks until such time as the picture is more clear. The world to-day, in my opinion, is in a fluid state, and those who are thinking in terms of regulating the currency and credit of this nation or of any other nation as it was prior to the outbreak of this war are not cognizant of the world situation. To-day international organizations are now talking about developing currency and credit in the international field for the exchange of goods and commodities between the different countries, and when that body lays down its mandate in that field it will affect the internal economy of every country, I do not care who is in power.
As I see the present proposals which the minister has brought in, and as I listen to and read the controversy that is taking place in the banking and commerce committee, it is all an indication to me at any rate, as a layman who makes no pretence at being an expert, that the whole matter of currency and credit is confused and requires a good deal of clarification.
The bills themselves and the discussions that I have listened to in the house are a clear indication that we require a lot of serious thinking on this matter of currency and credit, because, in my opinion, it is the kernel of the whole economic system, and unless that is sound we are in for much confused post-war planning. I think, and I believe the minister does also, that the measures are not going to be of very much value now during the

Farm Credit-Mr. Gillis
process of fighting the war; they are designed to take care of some of our post-war problems both in the field of reconstruction and industry and in the field of the stabilization of agriculture. If that is the purpose for which they are designed then I suggest that until such time as the international picture and the national picture as well are clearer than they are at the present moment, the banking committee would be well advised, instead of definitely deciding that this is the cure for our post-war ills, to undertake a close study and to come to a clear understanding of postwar problems. I suggest that they might take that view instead of deciding that this is the remedy.
Of course I realize that these measures can always be changed; but it must not be forgotten that this government is on the eve of an election and while they may have these measures passed now-
