I am not a prophet but I am taking this bill as it reads. Personally I cannot see any redress for the farmer under the bill, though I have read it carefully. What is the experience in Norway, Sweden, Finland and France in connection with agricultural credits? They have endeavoured to solve the problem, and I know the machinery now being set up, both in the field of industrial development and in the field of agricultural credits, is not new. It was tried in the countries I have mentioned. The idea is merely to endeavour to extend and to build for the future on a machine which in my opinion has crashed and is beyond repair. That is why I do not want to pin our post-war plans in either field on this kind of machinery. You are not making any changes. You are still vesting in the chartered banks the right to issue or to withhold loans if they so desire. On the other hand, the government is going to accept a certain percentage of risk on the aggregate loans. As I heard the matter discussed here, I was led to believe by some members that the government would accept ten per cent of the individual loan. According to the bill, it is the aggregate loan. I presume at the end of the year the banks would file a stat# ment with the minister that the aggregate loans under the measure, in their particular branch, amounted to so much. They may have defaulted to the extent of such and such an amount and the department then assumes ten per cent of the liability of the total loans outstanding in that branch. Well, that might run into a condderable amount of money. However, I am not concerned about that. What I am thinking about is this, that the government guarantees the loan and does so with the taxpayers' money; and if the taxpayers' money is to assume the risk either under the Industrial Development bank bill or under this legislation, then I think they should expect to receive some benefits from it.
My Tory friends to the right and some of the Conservative members on the other side are very much concerned when one speaks about government control or the socialization of finance. They get all hot and bothered about that. The solution of the problem of
Farm Credit-Mr. Gillis

reconstruction and rehabilitation has been handed to the minister and the government. Industry says, "You accept the risk and allow us to make profits." There is nothing that smacks so much of that so-called enterprise as that. That is not a system, because if the system under which we have lived in the past has lacked anything it has lacked system. It is the most haphazard, grab-as-you-go system that has ever been or could be evolved. Their reason for existing and for wanting to perpetuate their future is that they take risk in the field of investment. Neither in the field of industry nor in the field of agriculture are they going to assume any risk in the future.
As I see it, what we have here and what we are evolving is a managerial form of society with the government managing the country, taking the risk, providing the services and guaranteeing the profits to the fellow who is not obliged to do even the thinking in his own private enterprise.

speechtext: If we had that it would be a terrible country.

That is exactly what we have. If the hon. member cannot see it that is not my fault. That is exactly what we are building up. We are not so far away from it.
I said I was not an expert on banking or finance. I read these things and I try to apply some common sense to them. What I am afraid of is that we may do this in a hurry and make a mess of it. When the Industrial Development bank bill was before the house I said that we of this party want to see the people of Canada benefited by the future activities of our government. I have Reiterated time and time again that the thing we quarrel with is not what somebody else owns; that is immaterial. We have quarreled with the fact that the control exercised by the banks and industries of this country is complete control over the initiative and the wealth-creating means of the people themselves. Because of that control they are restricted. It is that control we want to unharness. We are not concerned with what the banks and industries have, but it is a fact that they can hold back the creative energies of the people in developing the country's resources for themselves.
The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) talked of being afraid of the approach of the city banker to the problem of the farmer who may require credit in a hurry. I absolutely agree with him, because you do not have to go back very far into history in so far as the banking field is concerned to see that. The province of Nova Scotia

is a very good illustration. Not so many years ago we had our own banks there. They were owned and managed by Nova Scotians to do Nova Scotia business. We had no difficulties. Then they were merged into a central institution, and to-day if you want to start a small factory or get a loan over $500 you have to go to some central headquarters and clearly define the purposes for which you require the loan. If you are starting something that comes in competition with something that is already tied in with that centre you do not get the money. You have lost control.
When I spoke on the Industrial Development bank bill I tried to focus attention on the possibilities of supporting and developing the credit union organizations across Canada. I think the hon. member for Macdonald struck the nail on the head when he expressed his fear. If there is any institution in Canada that could come to the rescue of the farmer it is the credit union institution, which has been established on a community basis. If the government of this country are prepared to use the taxpayers' money to subsidize or guarantee the loans of the chartered banks in this field, what is the matter with giving some assistance to a movement that is already established in the field?

speechtext:
I am not going to argue with the minister. The institution to which I refer is already well developed. Thousands and thousands of members have studied the movement. The farmer will require his immediate credits on a community basis. Short-term or intermediate credits are not the solutions of the fanner's problems. That is what has hamstrung him in the past. What he requires is long-term mortgage credit. If short-term and intermediate credit were the solution hundreds of farmers across the country would not have lost their properties. They lost their properties during the depression because they had short-term credits. If the government can protect them I think it should have protected the soldier settlers. It is only two weeks ago that we had a delegation from Manitoba and

Farm Credit-Mr. Gillis
Saskatchewan in this city pointing out to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) that since the outbreak of this war approximately 606 soldier settlers a year for the four war years in those provinces have lost their properties because of their inability to meet their payments. That has happened during this war. If there was a solution of the credit needs of the farmers of Canada the loss of property by farmers across the country would not have taken place. What the farmer needs is long-term and mortgage credit, not shortterm and intermediate credit, which has been the evil of the system in the past.
Many people think credit unions are small. They are not. Those unions consist of a large number of members, and the movement is a national one. There are 129 credit unions in Alberta, 108 in British Columbia, 78 in Manitoba, 146 in New Brunswick, 204 in Nova Scotia, 163 in Ontario, 47 in Prince Edward Island, 749 in Quebec and 128 in Saskatchewan, making a total of 1,759 across the country. These are only branches. There are thousands of members in this association pooling their resources on a community basis. To-day they control considerable finance across the country, and they have developed the field of credit to a very great extent. They have linked up the industrial worker and the rural worker on that basis. They meet together. They iron out their problems together. They are beginning to understand each other's problems.
What militates against that movement today is the lack of some central tie-up with the different provinces. It is tied up to some extent in Nova Scotia. It is coordinated with a credit union league, but it is not functioning to lend money on long-term loans or on mortgages. I emphasize the necessity of a national organization that would not only utilize the finances they have now but make use of the brains and the stamina that have been given by those who have voluntarily developed that organization across Canada in a completely new field.
They are not looking for anything for their services. The whole movement is voluntary. It aims at uplifting the intelligence of the people and solving this community credit problem which developed as a result of the failure of the banks to do anything about the matter back in the thirties. This organization has made wonderful progress, and I would suggest that when the banking and commerce committee come to study this bill they get the statistics which are available in connection with this movement and1 call in the people at the head of it to see if this organization cannot be utilized on a national basis for the
purpose of providing long-term mortgage credits for the farmers of this country. If the movement is not large enough to take care of the whole problem on a national scale it could be assisted and developed.
No money will be lost under this movement.
I happen to belong to this organization, which I helped set up in Nova Scotia. I have here a note from the manager of the credit union to which I belong. In the ten years during which the movement has been in operation in Nova Scotia it has not had one bad loan, and loans of up to $3,000 have been made by the local branches. This is just one branch, located in one ward of the town of Glace Bay, and the manager states that at the present time their assets amount to $60,000; that they have a savings account of $52,000, a loan balance of $41,000 and victory bonds to the extent of $8,200. This was just a note to let me know how the thing was going, since I was a member of the board of directors until I came here. As I say, this is just one small branch in one section of that community, and there are many others. In my opinion this offers a solution of the problem of farm credit in Canada. Under this set-up the farmer is dealing with his own people. If he meets adverse conditions and cannot live up to the terms of his agreement 100 per cent, he is not called in by a banker who is responsible to a board of directors in some distant city. Whether or not the bank manager is sympathetic-as I believe most of them are-he has no alternative but to squeeze the borrower, for the terms of a loan with a bank cannot be altered. Under this set-up, however, a man deals with his own people, who are not subject to a board of directors in Montreal or Toronto. His board of directors lives right in the community; they know him personally, and can extend his loan and perhaps waive his interest, simply because they are not paying salaries to people whose only function is to scrutinize the balance sheet at the end of the year.
Loans made through this medium are also protected by insurance. These unions insure their loan balance and share capital. According to this letter, which I am not going to bother reading but which I can show to the minister at any time he cares to look at it, their share capital is insured for sixty-five cents a hundred dollars and their loan balance for seventy-five cents a hundred dollars. The way it works, and the way it would work for the farmer, is this. If a man had $500 of share capital and wanted to take out that money as a loan, he would do so. Then he would make his purchase for cash, which means a saving of up to perhaps fifteen per
Farm Credit-Mr. Gillis

cent. Supposing something happens in the meantime; the man dies. That $500 is outstanding, but while he used that money that amount remains to his credit as share capital. In Nova Scotia at any rate that loan balance and share capital are insured through the Cuna Mutual Cooperative Insurance Company, which now has offices in Canada and is well established in the United States. That company pays off the loan balance and doubles the share capital to the beneficiary of the person involved in that loan. Many of the insurance companies cannot understand how they do it, but they do; we have had such cases ourselves. Under a set-up like that, with some assistance and encouragement from the federal government, a national organization could be developed to take care of the credit needs of farmers across Canada on a community basis. With this protection by insurance you cannot lose anything, but you will bring about a brand new economic reform in Canada in the field of finance and credit, while each individual member of the organization will benefit.
I am not going to discuss this matter longer; I am sorry to have taken up so much of the time of the house. I only want to emphasize that in view of the unsettled international situation, which is reflected in the situation of each country, with such important questions coming up for discussion as the renewal of the charters of the banks, the development of some form of credit for the farmers, the Industrial Development bank in connection with industry, all looking to the post-war period, it is my opinion that with the picture as confused as it is at present the banking and commerce committee would be well advised to take a year or so to study the set-up and bring in necessary reforms to the whole banking and credit structure, rather than make decisions now while the situation is in such turmoil. In my view this measure does not touch the problem at all; it will not do anything for the farmer as far as his credit needs are concerned. In the first place, short-term and intermediate credit caused many farmers to be dispossessed of their land in days gone by. What they require-and this is not my opinion but the opinion of men who have studied this matter-is long-term and mortgage credit if they are to be given an opportunity to utilize any lending institution in order to rehabilitate and maintain their farms. Short-term and intermediate credit is not the answer; it must be long-term and mortgage credit. There is a possibility of developing that field through the credit union set-up which now is organized nationally, and which has given this question a great deal of study.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Perhaps almost everything has been said on this bill that can be said, Mr. Speaker, but there are one or two thoughts which may not have been emphasized as much as I think they should be. I should like to give expression to a few of the facts which I think should be emphasized a good deal more, in the consideration of a matter of this kind. I do not think there is any division of opinion as to the farmer's need of additional equipment, improvements and alterations on his farm. However, what is the consequence of enabling him to make these provisions? I think that is something most hon. members have not followed through in their discussions on the bill.
This is a bill to give the farmer more ready access to credit, so as to enable him, for example, to acquire more farm machinery. Certainly if he is able to acquire more farm machinery and other equipment, he will be able to increase his production in proportion to the amount of equipment acquired. In other words, the result of this legislation, as well as the legislation setting up an industrial bank, and other similar legislation, is to stimu-

Farm Credit-Mr. Kuhl
late to still great heights the production of this country, whether it be primary, secondary or anything else.
The question I would ask at this point is this: Was the problem which faced the people of Canada before the war one of inability to produce? AVere -we lacking in production of anything? Was there any lack of production of farm commodities? Was there any lack of any commodities produced in Canada? The answer is obvious. We were being told on every hand before the war that our problem was one of overproduction. Everyone was saying that our problem was not one of production; rather it was the reverse.
Yet to-day we have before us a bill the purpose of which is to stimulate production to still higher levels in the post-war period. *If the problem is one of production, or if the distribution could be accomplished by the system of production we had before the war- and it was not accomplished-how do we expect it will be accomplished after the war, with the same principle involved? Before the war the people of Canada were not consuming all the production they desired. For example, lumber was sixth on our list of exports, prior to the war. Yet I am sure that every stick of that lumber could have been used in Canada, had the people been in a position to buy it. That applies not only to lumber, but to many other products, which were exported.
The point I make is that in the discussion on this bill, as in most discussions pertaining to the post-war period, the emphasis has been placed on the wrong aspect of our national life. Hon. members always emphasize the production end of our economy. That is absolutely wrong, because production has never been a problem with us. The problem has been one of distribution and consumption. As some of my colleagues have already indicated this afternoon, if a measure of this sort is to be of any real benefit to the farmers, or if any similar legislation is to be of benefit to any other section of our community, it will have to be accompanied by legislation of a different kind altogether, something far more fundamental.
I contend that this measure will be of practically no avail in helping farmers in the post-war world. There are some who have said that the legislation should be accompanied by other legislation providing floors under agricultural prices. I am heartily in accord with any action which would guarantee a higher income for the farmer. But the point we must not overlook is that if there are floor prices under the products of the farm, and if there are minimum wages, all those factors are again reflected in prices. All costs enter into
prices. As far as the aggregate is concerned, in those circumstances the people as a whole are no farther ahead. The mere setting of floor prices and minimum wages will not be sufficient. We shall have to go a good deal farther than that.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and his colleagues, along with members of the Progressive Conservative party, and all other orthodox thinkers will have to acknowledge the fact that since the industrial revolution, and particularly in the last twenty-five years, no primary, secondary or any other industry ever distributed purchasing power sufficient to buy back its own production. One finds that demonstrated if he examines the balance sheet of any industrial concern. Prices of commodities which come out of an institution are always in excess of the buying power coming from that institution. Therefore the aggregate for the nation as a whole is identical with that of one institution. It follows that the emphasis in respect of post-war legislation should be placed on the consuming end of our economy.
If consumption is taken care of, production will take care of itself. The house constantly concerns itself with the production end; but I am satisfied that if the government would introduce legislation enabling consumers to buy up to the limit of their desire to consume, we would have no problem at all in connection with financing production. But so long as we constantly hope and anticipate that our present income, or the income which will obtain after the war, will distribute the goods produced from industry, so long as we base all our hopes on that kind of thinking, all legislation of this kind is bound to fall far short of what is anticipated.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) made some observations respecting the ability of credit unions to provide what he considered was the type of credit farmers require. I believe he went so far as to suggest that the credit unions principle was the solution of farmers' problems. Perhaps he would go so far as to say that it would also be the solution of the problem of many other members of our society.
I support the idea of credit unions, but not for the same reason as that offered by the hon. member. I believe he is labouring under a delusion in respect of what is accomplished by credit unions. After all, a credit union is just a savings bank, or a reinvestment of savings. If I take $100 out of my earnings and put it into a credit union, that $100 is represented by $100 worth of goods somewhere on the shelves. If I do not buy that $100 worth of goods and pay my money into the credit union, then that $100 worth of goods remains
Farm Credit-Mr. Bryce

on the shelf. If someone else uses my $100 and puts it into new production, that $100 produces another $100 worth of goods. So that there are now two lots of goods, but only one lot of purchasing power. That is the result of the use of the credit union. I agree that it is good as far as it goes, but I certainly cannot grant that it is the solution of the problem of the farmer, of the labouring man or of other world problems.
We should emphasize the consumer end of our economy. Take care of the consumer and the production side will take care of itself. What we need is new credit and not the redistribution of old credit. We are short as it is. In normal times we are. short at least forty cents or perhaps fifty cents on the dollar. When we consider the degree to which machinery will be substituted for man-power when the war is over we must realize there will be a further deficiency in our purchasing power.
If the government, or the Progressive Conservative party for that matter, rely on legislation of this kind as a means of coping with the problems of the post-war world, they will be sadly disillusioned before many days go by. They will eventually come to the place where they will agree that the only solution is that which has been advocated by the Social Crediters of Canada and of the world, namely, to supply the consumer with buying power to enable him to buy up to the limit of his desire to consume. Until that is done, we shall fall far short of arriving at a solution of our problems.
If the members of the government and those who are like-minded want to continue bumping their heads against a stone wall until they learn, that is their right, but personally I can see the handwriting on the wall and I am satisfied that there will be no solution of these post-war problems that will provide individual liberty as well as security unless it involves new credit to stimulate consumption rather than production.

Mr. Speaker, I understand from my colleagues that this is the last opportunity I shall have to speak on this matter, and I should like to add a few words to what I said yesterday. I said yesterday that it was absolutely necessary that legislation of this kind should contain a crop failure clause. If we analyse conditions we find that on many occasions the farmer has been accused of not paying his bills. That is wrong because the farmer more than any other person in this country is gambling with the elements. If he does not get a return for his labour, how can he pay his bills?

The banker is protected because when a man cannot pay his bill in the fall he is carried over to another year and he has still more to pay. He is faced with compound interest. The farmers are willing to pay. I am a farmer, and a small one at that. I know that you cannot pay your debts if you do not have money coming in. It is the business of the farmer to gamble with the elements all the time.
A man may decide to put in a concrete floor or some other improvement and spread it over three years, as is suggested in the bill. But if he does not get a crop, he will not be able to pay. I have the assurance of the minister that he will consider including a crop failure clause in the bill.

What I said was that I
would see it was given consideration in the banking and commerce committee when this bill is referred to that committee.

speechtext:
I would suggest that the
provision with regard to live stock should include bees. A number of years ago I could buy bees for $1.95 a package, and to-day I must pay $5. If I bought a hundred packages before, I paid $200, but to-day I must pay $500. The farmers need assistance there and I ask that that be included.
If a man borrows money to buy a binder and because of crop failure he is unable to repay it, I do not think it is right that the bank can come along and take a couple of cows to pay for the binder. If I make a deal on a binder, the binder should stand by itself. I do not think I want to take up any more of the time of the house as long as I have the assurance of the minister that he will look after these two points.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have one or two thoughts I should like to leave with the minister for his consideration. This bill has reference to farming operations from the man's point of view. There is nothing in it that looks at the problem of farming from the woman's point of view. If you are to have successful, contented and happy farm people, the farmer's wife must feel that way about farming. I suggest that section 2, paragraph (a) should cover not only electrical equipment but plumbing and heating and modern sanitary facilities. These things play a large part in the contentment of the people who farm.
The next paragraph should make provision for washing machines, modern stoves and heating equipment. Why provide all the facilities for the male side of the partnership and not give some consideration to the female

Farm Credit

Mr. Edwards
side of the farming operations? I am also concerned about paragraph (i) of section 1, which defines "farmer" as follows:
"Farmer" means a person who is in possession of a farm . . .
Does that mean physical possession or legal possession? A similar term has been the subject of a great deal of controversy and it seems to me that this paragraph ought to be clarified. I think actual residence on the farm is what is contemplated. I believe it is intended that this legislation shall benefit the man actually on the farm, the man who is working at farming as such. Then I would refer to section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (f) which reads:
the rate of interest charged by the bank on the loan did not exceed five per centum per annum simple interest as long as the borrower was not in default.
I think there ought to be some limitation to cover the situation where the farmer is in default. Most of the trouble of our farmers in western Canada in buying machinery and equipment has been that the lien note stated "five per cent until default." Then what? It read all the way from eight to twelve or fourteen per cent. I think there ought to be some limitation, some ceiling, on the rate of interest which the bank can charge when the note becomes in default.
The other point is as to the limit of the liability. Section 3 states:
The minister shall, subject to the provisions of this section and of the two next following sections, pay to a bank the amount of loss sustained by it as a result of a farm improvement loan . . .
And it provides for the government paying ten per cent of the loss sustained. But what is to be included in the term "loss"? The principal sum advanced? The principal, plus accumulated interest? Are legal costs to be included? Are fire, sickness or accident insurance premiums that may have been paid in connection with the loan to be included? I think the term "loss" ought to be clarified to a much greater degree than it now is.
Then section 3, subsection 1, paragraph (b), states:
the application stated that the borrower held an interest in the farm of the nature prescribed for the class of farm improvement loans to which such loan belongs.
I cannot for the life of me make out what is the nature of the interest. Is a tenant to be entitled to borrow? Does he state his interest as a tenant? Is a purchaser under an agreement for sale entitled to borrow? Does he state his interest as a purchaser under an agreement for sale? Are you to have your loans classified according to the nature of the interest held; that is to say, that a tenant will
be able to borrow up to a certain amount or on certain things and that the holder of possession under an agreement for sale will be able to borrow certain limited sums and for certain specified purposes? The section is not clear to me, and I should be glad if the minister would elucidate just what is contemplated by that phrase "held an interest in the farm".

the construction, repair or alteration of, or making of additions to, any building or structure on a farm.
Household chattels are beyond the scope of the bill, and are intended to be; but if some good reason were adduced for including them, that would be a matter for the consideration of the banking and commerce committee. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Yes; there is an argument there. That is a matter that can be considered in committee.
Several members have taken exception to the rate of five per cent and suggested that the rate should be four or three per cent, but five per cent is lower than the ordinary rate charged at the present time and, as I indicated in a previous debate, if the limit is too low I do not think we can expect the freedom to lend that we otherwise could on the part of the banks. As one hon. member said, you can ask the banks to lend but you cannot make them lend. A fair rate of interest will have to be fixed, having regard to the protection which the government gives to banking institutions.
That raises the other question as to whether ten per cent is too low and whether it should be twenty per cent. In practice there comes a point beyond which one might as well make it 100 per cent as anything above that point. In other words, if the principle of the bill is to be to eliminate risk entirely from the banks and say that they should lend to anybody who applies for a loan, and that we shall make good any loss that is sustained, then the banks take no risk whatever. I do not think the house will approve a bill of that kind; I do not think I would be in favour of it; in fact I know I would not. The banks must exercise some real judgment in the selection of risks under the scheme. It is a matter of judgment on the part of parliament as to where they should put

the percentage of guarantee. We put it at fifteen per cent in the home improvement plan and found that considerably higher than necessary, and we thought ten per cent was ample for this scheme. The losses under the home improvement plan were less than one per cent of the total amount lent, and we would be exposing ourselves to severe criticism, I believe, if we placed the percentages so high that the banks would not be taking any risks at all.

maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: There must be a happy medium somewhere.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: After all, this is still private enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARM CREDIT
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Yes. That is a very just observation. The banks are carrying on under the system of private enterprise and they must take some risk. The total removal of risk from private enterprise is justified only if there is a very strict limitation of profit indeed, perhaps the elimination of profit. I have not just thought that through.
There have been various suggestions that the banks should not be empowered to enforce security on the loan. If they are not to be empowered to enforce it they should not be empowered to take it. If they are empowered to take it they should be empowered to enforce it. The one follows the other. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) did not object to the taking of security so long as they could not enforce it. That is a very happy and irresponsible position to take. It is popular with everyone. The borrower could get a loan because he could offer security, but when it came to making good on his obligation nothing could be done against him because the banks could not enforce security. That, of course, is not a matter that needs to be argued about further. If the banks are not empowered to take security fewer loans will be made than otherwise would be the case.
It is a question how far we think we should go in facilitating and encouraging lending to farmers in the period ahead of us. We had a feeling that we should facilitate it to a considerable degree. The farmers would be needing a lot of intermediate loans, and shortterm loans are pretty well provided for now under the Bank Act as it stands; long-term loans are provided for in other ways by the Canadian Farm Loan Board Act, by the lending institutions of the country, the loan and trust companies. But there is a gap in the credit structure for farmers just as there is for industries, and we are trying to fill the gap in the case of industries by setting up the Industrial Development bank, and for the reasons I state we felt that rather than set up

Farm Credit-Mr. Ilsley
an agricultural bank, with thousands of branches and a large personnel, it would be better to meet the problem in the way we have attempted to meet it by this bill.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) advanced an interesting theory, that because we were supplying these facilities for loans other lenders would withdraw and perhaps we would hurt the farmer more than we helped him. I cannot follow that. I think he was mixed up between the operations of the farm loan board and the operations of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. It is probably true that the operations of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in eastern Canada discouraged lending by persons who otherwise would be lending money on mortgage on farm properties. I think it did. I believe that was the case in eastern Canada, but I do not think the existence of the Canadian farm loan board has done that. I do not think the existence of these facilities would do it.
I have noted the observations with regard to the credit failure clauses and have given the assurance that these suggestions will be considered in committee.
The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) asked a question as to whether the bankers would give the farmers good service. Before the banking and commerce committee the general managers of the banks, or most of them, will undoubtedly appear, and will give evidence. That committee ought to get just as definite a forecast as they can from the general managers as to how they propose to act in the operation of the scheme, and I think they will be able to get convincing assurances.
While probably it would not be possible for the head office to dictate in detail the action which the managers would take, I think that, with efficient institutions such as the chartered banks of Canada, the spirit in which the measure is to be administered would be pretty well known before very long and all managers would conduct themselves accordingly.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) suggested that the credit unions should have the same privileges as the banks. He touched on that. I interjected the remark that they are not under our jurisdiction at all. I do not believe that they are under federal jurisdiction. They are organized under provincial jurisdiction and are not subject to inspection by the federal insurance department or ;by the finance department, and we have no way of supervising the system of loaning of this kind. The hon. member went on to say that, apart from assistance by the government, the credit unions were the people to solve the problem and that they could solve
it. I do not agree with him. I think that if we wait until the capital goes into the credit unions to supply the needs of the borrowing farmers of Canada we shall wait a good deal longer than the year he suggests-a great many years. Moreover, the credit unions charge more in the way of interest rates than is proposed under this measure. I do not think it is a practical suggestion.

speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question, and I want him to understand that I am seeking information only. When he spoke on this matter yesterday, as reported at page 3645 of Hansard, he pointed out that no railway issues have been sold since the outbreak of war, and also that these securities might be sold either to the government or to the public. maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION

speechtext:
Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of bill No. 135, to provide regulations enabling Canadian war service electors to exercise their franchise, and Canadian prisoners of war to vote by proxy, at any general election held during the present war, also to provide amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, which are consequential to such regulations, or have become necessary by the advent of the said war.
36SS
Dominion Elections Act

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 1-War services electors voting at a general election.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: I think the minister ought to make a statement at some stage of the bill and perhaps this would be an appropriate time to hear what he has to say.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when one bears in mind the fact that concurrence in the committee's report was waived and that the bill passed its second reading without debate 1 think I should accept the invitation of the leader of the opposition and say a few words at this stage. As the committee is aware, this bill is the result of some labour on the part of a special committee. I believe it will be gratifying to the committee to know that the report of the special committee was unanimous. I believe it was unanimous for two reasons. First, we had as chairman the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Factor), and I think all members of the committee were impressed with his industry and above all the fair-minded attitude with which he approached the problem.
In the second place, I think I can say that eveiy hon. member of the special committee approached his task with only one object in view, to ensure the fullest opportunity being provided to those in the service forces of Canada to exercise their franchise. I know that all those who sat with me on the committee will agree when I say that there was no effort on the part of anyone to secure any petty political advantage, that politics in the narrow sense of that word were not even considered in the result arrived at.
I believe that this report represents as fair and intelligent a solution of this problem as has been presented in any democratic nation. The committee had the benefit of the services of Mr. Harry Butcher, K.C., once an esteemed member of this house and one who I believe is generally regarded, along with the chief electoral officer, as probably knowing more about electoral matters than any other citizen in Canada. The committee went at its work with considerable care.
It had the advantage of the legislation passed in Great Britain. It also had for consideration the legislation passed in the various provinces of Canada where such legislation has been enacted. Consideration was also given to the legislation passed in Australia under which the last federal election in that commonwealth was held and to the legislation of New Zealand and South Africa.

In addition the committee considered the legislation now being discussed in the United States. While that was a matter of interest, its actual benefit on account of different electoral methods was not so great. I recall that some method was placed before the committee dealing with the federal election held in 1864 during the civil war when the votes were actually taken upon the battlefield.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
You did not neglect the
past.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
We were very careful to consider both the past and the present, although perhaps the present was more in our minds. But because of their different electoral system, the practical advantages of the United States legislation was very small.
Perhaps I may now deal with the bill itself. As will be noted, the bill is not an amendment to the elections act of 1938; it is a new bill. It deals with matters of immediate importance in connection with active service voters, and to that extent it will be in force and effect for the duration of the war and six months thereafter. But it deals also with a number of matters which will be operative after that period of time, and for those reasons it was felt it would be better to have a new bill rather than amendments to the elections act, 1938.
The bill has two schedules, A and B. Schedule A deals with those in the armed 'orces and in the auxiliary services, while schedule B deals with prisoners of war. Schedule A was gone over word for word and approved by the special committee. At the time the committee reported and suggested that the voting of prisoners of war be done by proxy schedule B had not been considered section by section, but it is the result of the committee's recommendations and now appears in the form of fifteen sections in the schedule-.
I believe the definition of war service voter will be found to be very broad since it covers not only those in the navy, army and air force but also, subject to conditions which the committee will want to discuss, those in the auxiliary services. It covers those in the mercantile marine and any Canadian on any ship of Canadian or British registry or the registry of any country allied with His Majesty in the present war. The question of age is immaterial as far as an elector serving in the active forces is concerned. Only one qualification is required, namely, that the elector be a British subject. In the case of certain auxiliary services and organizations it is necessary that the electors be stationed outside the boundaries of Canada. In other

Dominion Elections Act
words, it w'as felt that there should be the widest possible definition in order that everyone who is contributing to the defence of Canada and the prosecution of this war shall be ensured the right to exercise either his or her franchise.
It was necessary to provide machinery for the taking of the direct vote, in the one case, and the proxy vote, in the other. There is one quite material change being made in the elections act. Instead of seven days elapsing to permit papers as well as the names of candidates to be forwarded to the special returning officers, there will be a period of twenty-eight days allowed. In other words, there will be twenty-eight days between the official nominations and polling day.
The bill provides for the appointment of special returning officers in each major district, there being five in Canada. It makes provisions also for special returning officers in Newfoundland and Great Britain. Power is given to the chief electoral officer to recommend to the government, and ta the government to appoint special returning officers in such other theatres of war as may be thought necessary. This machinery can be more fully dealt with when we come to the particular sections.
I am told by the chief electoral officer that notwithstanding the fact that the votes will have to be counted and taken in widely separated portions of the world, the time that will elapse from the issue of the writs of election until election day will not be more than sixty days. In addition to that, whereas in the last war it required at least two months to get results from the ballots overseas and three months before a definite declaration as to the successful candidate could be made, under the procedure adopted by the committee it will be possible for these results to be secured within eight days.
There may be other points that I might have dealt with, but I believe I have indicated the general features of the bill that is now before the committee. It is not claimed that this bill is fool-proof. It will require a certain measure of cooperation and a large measure of intelligent work in its operation. What is claimed, however, both in the breadth of its definition of those who can vote as war service electors and in the plan for giving votes to prisoners of war is that it is probably the broadest measure adopted by any country in the British commonwealth of nations.
It is also claimed that the special committee set about its task for the sole purpose of securing that no one would be deprived of his or her vote if it was humanly possible to enable him to register it and that each
would preserve the right of franchise in determining who would form the government of Canada for the duration of the war and, we trust, for the years that follow after it.

speechtext: In order to conduct an election within sixty days after dissolution, is it not the government's intention to ask for the right, if they have not the right at present, to arrange for the naming of special returning officers at once so that everything will be in readiness to carry out the election within the short space of sixty days after dissolution?

bill but rather to what is not in this bill. I was a member of the special committee and I am in accord with the regulations as drafted and embodied in the bill. There was one matter, however, which I think the committee should have included in its deliberations, though perhaps not in the regulations as drafted. I think the committee should have presented a recommendation to the house with respect to acquainting those in the armed services with the issues upon which they would be called upon to ballot. With the war situation as it is now in Europe, with things pretty much uprooted and a very confused picture over there, this is not just the kind of setting that I would choose to discuss this matter. But the regulations are here. I think one of the most important things is that those in the services who are to cast their ballots should have some knowledge of the issues on which they are to vote. The thing I was concerned about in the regulations, as I started to say, was to give those in the service who were to ballot some idea as to what they were to ballot on. The regulations themselves are clear and specific in so far as the candidate is concerned, his occupation and so forth. I did think, however, the committee might have recommended to the house something similar to what was done in New Zealand. I proposed that to the committee, but they did not see eye-to-eye with me on it. The drafting of a manifesto giving each party who may have candidates in the election an opportunity of briefly setting out the basic principles for which they stand is something desirable; and failing that, if the committee were not prepared to recommend it I thought, and some of the members of the committee agreed, that there was a possibility of utilizing the Canadian Press service. There is now established by the Canadian Press a

Dominion Elections Act
news service in the form, I believe, of an eight-page paper which is widely circulated throughout the different services both in England and in the Mediterranean, 'and I presume that when lines are established it will be on the European continent; that is, if we do not go through there very fast, as I hope we shall. I thought there might be a possibility of taking the last four or five weeks prior to the election and, by some arrangement with the Canadian Press, each party who may have candidates in the field could be privileged to use a column or so for the purpose of setting out what they stand for in this election and developing the issues as they saw fit. In that way there would be no cost; "there would be no responsibility on the part of the government. I thought in connection with the regulations I would raise that matter in the house in order to determine whether hon. members were desirous of going to that extent at least in informing those in the service as to what they were balloting on. I believe that those in the armed services to-day are fighting for something; every man there is fighting for social objectives in addition to defeating those who would lay down a totalitarian system throughout the world. We in Canada are framing legislation to which they are to come back. The kind of Canada we build here, through the medium of this House of Commons and our provincial legislatures, is the framework into which these boys will fit when they come back. It is not going far enough simply to day down regulations, and as far as possible put the ballot into the hands of the service personnel, unless at the same time we are prepared to give information, in so far as it is possible for us to do so, as to what each candidate they will ballot on stands for.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
I shall be able to do that, but unfortunately the memorandum I have-
I would not want to trust my memory to do it -is perhaps a little longer than should be required, but if it is the wish of the committee, I shall read it. It is as follows:
There appears to be some misapprehension with regard to the secrecy of the ballot paper prescribed by the proposed regulations for use by war service electors at the next general election.
The procedure prescribed by the said regulations is similar to that followed for the taking of the votes of members of the active service forces of Canada at the 1940 general election and at the 1942 dominion plebiscite. On each of these occasions, not a single complaint was received that the manner in which ballot papers were marked by any active service electors was ascertained by voting officials or other persons. It may even be stated that it was generally considered that the prevailing special voting procedure afforded a higher degree of secrecy than the procedure prescribed for taking the vote of civilian electors.
I might explain that this is a memorandum of the chief electoral officer, and was not dictated by myself. It continues:
The proposed regulations prescribe that each \va r service elector before being allowed to vote will be required to make, before the commissioned officer designated to take such vote, a declaration on the back of the outer envelope in which his ballot paper will be transmitted by mail to the appropriate special returning officer. In such declaration the war service elector will state his name, rank and regimental number, together with the name of the place where he ordinarily resided prior to his enlistment, and other necessary particulars.
When the above declaration has been completed and signed by both the war service elector and the commissioned officer concerned, a ballot paper will be handed to the elector who will be allowed to mark it in private. The ballot paper will then be folded and placed in an inner envelope and after this envelope has been sealed bv the elector, it will be handed to the commissioned officer who, in full view of the elector, will place the inner envelope in the completed outer envelope above referred to. When the outer envelope has been sealed by the commissioned officer, it will be handed to the
elector who will himself dispatch it by mail to the special returning officer whose full name and address are printed on the face of such outer envelope.
When the outer envelopes reach their destination, they will be received by the special returning officer and his staff, mainly composed of six scrutineers nominated by the leaders of the various political parties.
Each outer envelope will then be sorted to its proper electoral district, according to the place of ordinary residence given by the elector in his declaration, by a pair of scrutineers consisting of persons representing different and opposed political interests, and no such envelope will be opened until the time has come to count all the ballot papers sorted to such electoral district. When the correct electoral district of a war service elector has been ascertained, the scrutineers will write the name of such electoral district on the back of the outer envelope and affix their initials thereto before sorting the outer envelope to its electoral district.
Voting by war service electors will take place on the twelve week days immediately preceding polling day and it is expected that outer envelopes containing the ballot papers cast by war service electors will be received by every special returning officer during a period of between twelve and fourteen days. At the end of each of such days all the outer envelopes sorted to a given electoral district will be placed, unopened, in a large envelope which will be specially sealed. At least two scrutineers will be required to affix their signatures to such seals.	_
These specially sealed large envelopes will remain in safe custody, unopened, until the ballot papers enclosed in them are counted, and the scrutineers are authorized by the regulations to inspect any or all such envelopes when they so desire.
The counting of the votes of war service electors will not begin until six o'clock p.m. on polling day. Then each pair of scrutineers will count the ballot papers, but for only one electoral district at a time. All the specially sealed large envelopes belonging to such electoral district will be opened and the outer envelopes contained therein will be placed on a table. After having ascertained that each of such outer envelopes belongs to the electoral district for which the ballot papers are being counted, the scrutineers will open each of such outer envelopes and place the unopened inner envelopes contained therein in a locked ballot box.
When all the inner envelopes sorted to a given electoral district have thus been placed in the ballot box, the ballot papers contained in the inner envelopes lose their identity, as these inner envelopes are absolutely plain.
When all the inner envelopes sorted to a given electoral district have been placed in the ballot box, the box will be unlocked by the special returning officer, and its contents will be placed upon a table. The scrutineers will then proceed to open such inner envelopes and count the ballot papers cast for each candidate officially nominated in such electoral district.
It will be observed that outer and inner envelopes containing ballot papers cast by war service electors are kept very carefully sealed up until the counting of the votes commences in the electoral district for which such envelopes have been sorted.
It will be observed also that every operation in the office of the special returning officer relating to the sorting and counting of the votes

Dominion Elections Act

cast by war service electors will be performed exclusively by scrutineers representing different political interests under the supervision of the special returning officer. A procedure of this kind should provide a maximum of secrecy to the ballot papers cast by war service electors.

As to the second point, I imagine that the hon. member was not in the chamber when I made my introductory remarks. Your committee further recommends that every person who, while on active service with the naval, military or air forces of Canada, became a prisoner of war and is officially recorded as such at headquarters, shall be entitled to vote by proxy, on a special certificate issued by the chief electoral officer. The fifteen clauses contained in schedule B were not considered word for word by the committee, but I believe they will be found to be a fair interpretation of the recommendation of the committee to enable the next of kin of prisoners of war provided they are

qualified electors, to vote by proxy in the particular riding in which the next of kin is a qualified elector at the time of the election.

speechtext: The minister has outlined how the balloting will take place. The elector will mark his ballot and place it in the inner envelope, which he will seal and then give to the officer commanding, who will put it in a large envelope in the presence of the elector. That large outer envelope will be sealed and given back to the elector, who will mail it. Now comes the point about which I w'ant to ask. How is that envelope mailed? Is it sent by the elector in an open mail bag, or is it put into a ballot box like those we use in the general elections here, on which there are locks?

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: I must say that I cannot answer that question; I do not know. I presume the procedure may be different in various areas. You see, there will be the special returning officers. maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: Look at form 10 on page 37; the information is contained there.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION

A good deal of misrepresentation may occur because of that. Some uniform regulation or practice should be adopted. It may be a mail bag which is locked, with some sort of opening which would just permit the envelope to go in. I feel, however, that some way should be devised whereby there could be no interference whatsoever with the ballot, once the elector drops it into the mail bag. I am sure there will be some objection or some complaints made after the election, especially if it is just an open box into which the ballot can be dropped by the elector. The war service elector shall then mail the completed outer envelope in the nearest post office or mail box.
I doubt if it would be of advantage to insist upon the Post Office Department providing certain equipment for the transmission of mail from the various points. speechtext: Section 35 of schedule A deals with the matter and sets it out clearly.

I think it is only fair to give a report of what certain members of the legion feel about the outer envelope. I, myself, am in favour of it. I think it is a safeguard and a protection. Certain members of the legion seem to think the outer envelope would permit the ascertaining of how a soldier might cast his vote. The outer envelope has his name and rank, and all particulars on it. Men who have written to me seem to think that would enable one to find out how a soldier voted. If the authorities take time to examine the envelopes, the outer envelope containing the inner envelope, I should imagine it would take a year to do so. I do not think anyone would do that. The argument used is that all that should be required of the soldier is that he come forward with his pay book. Hon. members on this side of the house who are in the armed forces will be familiar with the pay book. Each soldier carries a pay book, and it is said that presentation of same should be sufficient to obtain his ballot.
Dominion Elections Act

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION

I refer the committee to form 8 on page 35 that pertains to the outer envelope. The hon. member for Vancouver North, lately back from the front, served on the committee, and it paid a good deal of attention to what he said. He was in accord with these regulations. I listened to him carefully, and after his presentation I thought that what the ' committee adopted, namely, the programme of having an outer and inner envelope, was the best one.
May I say further that I have implicit confidence in the chief electoral officer. He has held that post for some years, and on any occasion I have made inquiries from him I have found him 100 per cent above-board. I am prepared to accept what he has presented. I believe it is the best elections act of any countiy in the world to-day, and I am convinced the chief electoral officer deserves more credit for it than does anybody else. He was always open to reason or to argument, and did not try at any time to influence the committee. The committee asked him on various occasions to explain details, and at all times, in my judgment, his explanations were satisfactory. I cannot see the objection to the inner and the outer envelope. Once the inner envelope is taken out of the outer envelope and placed in the ballot box, there is no possible way of telling whose ballot it might be. The outer envelope is certainly a check to control the voting, and a check against spurious voting, and against any stuffing of ballot boxes, or anything like that. No one has convinced me thus far that the procedure of using outer and inner envelopes is not a satisfactory one.

I do not think there is an argument or an objection which could be raised which is not covered in the regulations, if we read them through carefully.
Then, with respect to suspicion in some quarters, or the apprehension that the ballot may not be a secret one, may I say that I had two letters asking me-

Someone was leading the people in my section of the country to believe that the ballot would not be secret. I wrote back giving an explanation, and I recieved no further objections. They said, "If you are satisfied with it, it must be all right."

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
I will admit that the
hon. member was a real watch-dog.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
The memorandum read by the minister and prepared by the chief electoral officer sets out the procedure in detail. It is rather lengthy, however, and could be misunderstood. That is, anyone who might read it, and who might not understand the background of the committee's deliberations, might not understand it.
May I say, as a member of the special committee that the members belonging to this group after checking this over-and I discussed it with them as we went along-are perfectly satisfied with the regulations. In so far as the secrecy of the ballot is concerned, I am convinced there is no way of interfering with that ballot. The regimental number, the name of the voter and the constituency to which the ballot is directed will be written on the outside of the envelope and this leads some people to believe that when the envelope is opened the ballot can be checked. In this respect, therefore, it is different from the procedure followed in the Ontario election, in which the next of kin or the person designated who cast the vote had to have something official by way of proxy from the man concerned. I take it that under our procedure, whether or not a prisoner of war wants to vote, his next of kin may exercise the franchise for him if they so desire, without any direction or instruction on his part as to whether or not he desires his ballot to be cast.
I raise no objection to that; I merely point out what appears to be the dissimilarity between these regulations and those which were promulgated in connection with the Ontario election. As the minister knows, that experiment in the province was rather an unhappy one, and I am glad no suggestion has been made during the discussion of this bill that proxy voting, as it was carried on in Ontario, should be repeated during the federal election as far as our active service voters are concerned.
I hardly see how the regulations could be drawn differently, because of security matters and so on which might be involved if prisoners of war were asked to take some part in an election in a democratic state. I presume that point had some bearing and was a factor in the 
decision reached by the committee in regard to this point. I do not rise to complain, but only to point out the difference.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
I should like to ask one question about the next of kin voting. Supposing a soldier goes overseas and marries, and is then made a prisoner of war. Who is then his next of kin, as far as this vote is concerned?
Mr. MeLARTY: The wife is the next of kin:

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
But she is in England.
Mr. MeLARTY: It is the one appearing as next of kin on the records at headquarters.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
And a resident of Canada.
Mr. MeLARTY: And who is a qualified elector in the-constituency in which the proxy wishes to vote.

Section agreed to.
Schedule B agreed to.
On schedule A.
On section 35-War service elector voting as civilian.
Mr. MeLARTY: We have covered everything except this section. I have been giving the matter some little consideration, at least as much as could be given while dealing with the other sections. I realize that, as the leader of the opposition points out, there may be some cases-I should say they would be isolated cases-which will not be covered by the provisions concerning voting as a civil elector and the wide provisions covering voting as a service elector which, as the hon. member for Vancouver North pointed out, allow twelve days. It may be impossible to have polling booths as conveniently located for service electors as for civilian voters. On the other hand I must urge, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Yale, that hard cases make bad law. If one tries to cover too many exceptional cases he might stretch the bill to an unreasonable length.
I suggest to the hon. member that the number of exceptions there will be, in the instance to which he has directed attention, are not numerous. On the other hand, in considering just how to give effect to those few odd cases, I must say frankly that unless we are prepared to enlarge greatly the number of polling subdivisions for war service electors, I do not see that there is any possibility of doing it. Consequently I feel that unless my hon. friend insists, not seeing any way out of the difficulty, and believing that the difficulty will be met with only in most

exceptional cases, we might proceed. I am wondering if it is of sufficient importance to hold up the committee.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Perhaps we can dispose
of it readily. I take it that the minister has indicated the government's position. If the government desires to take the responsibility -as it must, in the end, in any event-and feels that the section must go through as it is, then I can only say that I can accept no responsibility whatsoever for agreeing to a section of this kind. I must confess that I think we should have taken much more time. The bill was presented only this afternoon, and I think we ought to have had some time to consider the matter raised. So far the bill has passed with very little discussion, the reason being that the Votes and Proceedings have carried the general provisions.
I say that the minister and the government are asking far too much when they ask the opposition to give consent, without further consideration. If the government decides to take that stand, and accept that responsibility, then it may do so. But it certainly is carried over the most vehement and vigorous protest, so far as I am concerned.

maintopic: MEASURE TO ENABLE WAR SERVICE PERSONNEL TO VOTE IN GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
I am quite agreeable to allowing the section to stand.
Section stands.
Schedule A stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext: I have read this section with a good deal of interest and I see that certain regulations, certain methods, and certain points in connection with courts martial are laid down here, but a great deal is omitted with regard to the conduct of courts martial, and I must presume, therefore, that they come under the regulations. maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866

maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT

maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
What would be the nature of the case which the accused would bring to the court? Would he sue someone for damages?

Naval Service Act

maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866

speechtext: No; that has not been put in the bill. There is at the present time an order in council establishing the naval board, and it is proposed to put that in the regulations. It is more or less a matter of internal administration in the department which, perhaps, at some future time may be changed. Some other minister might prefer some other title for his advisers; consequently it was not thought right to incorporate that in a statute. It will be in the regulations.

maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: I understand that there has been acquiesence on the part of the government with the criticisms which were made last year by Commander MacLean with respect to the suggestion of the inclusion of two extra members from the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve on the naval board. Could the minister advise us whether or not there was an addition to the board, and, if so, were naval volunteer reserve men appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
In the first place I would not say that it was 'because of Commander MacLean's protestations or statements that the change was made. I think the hon. member for Lake Centre, my hon. friend's colleague, made a well reasoned plea on that point at one time in the house when my estimates were up, which impressed me considerably. But apart from that, the naval reserve and the naval volunteer reserve have now grown to such proportions that it was felt we should give them fuller representation on the board, and that
was done by means of an amendment to the original order in council establishing the board.

maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
I was not trying to assess the position in which the minister found himself as regards the representations which were made. I was merely inquiring, because I have just read in the magazine edited by Commander MacLean of a suggestion of that kind.
In conclusion, may I say that a very interests ing situation may have escaped the notice of the members of the committee to-night. While we were discussing the Naval Services Act the navy was represented by the minister who was sponsoring the bill. One of the chief critics on our side of the house was the former Minister of National Defence, and the acting chairman of the committee was no less than a flight lieutenant of the Royal Canadian Air Force (Mr. Sinclair); therefore, the three services were represented on this particular occasion. I thought the committee might like to have that drawn to its attention at this time.

maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
Before the last section
passes, may I ask a question with reference to section 115? I realize that the section has already passed. According to this section the minister may order a penalty remitted or suspended. I presume that would be a sentence passed by the judge advocate, or whatever is the proper name. Would the minister have the power to override a judge's decision?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: The minister always has power to reduce a sentence, yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
May I ask a question
about another section that has been passed?
Should there not be a qualifying phrase in section 2 (b) similar to that found in paragraphs (c) and (g)? My point in asking that question will be obvious. Provision is made in paragraphs (c) and (g) for the occasion when under the Department of National Defence Act there is a minister and deputy minister of national defence for naval services. I wonder whether paragraph (b) should not have a similar qualifying phrase, so that the department under that same circumstance would mean, not the Department of National Defence but the Department of National Defence for Naval Services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
The hon. member raises an interesting point; but I am advised, and I think my advice is correct that the draftsmanship is right. By looking at the National Defence Act itself and the amending act of July 12, 1940, I conclude that the paragraph is in proper form.
370S
Naval Service Act

Strictly speaking, there is only one Department of National Defence. My colleague, the Minister for Air and I are merely named as ministers of national defence for air and national defence for naval services. No special department is named. Consequently I think it is better that we should be correct and have the word "department" defined as it is now, to mean only the Department of National Defence. It is a good point; I am glad my hon. friend raised it, but on reflection I think the paragraph is correctly worded.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext: I just wanted to be sure it was not an error.

maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the leader of the opposition has made reference to you, with your very distinguished service in the air, taking part in the passing of this naval bill, and also to my colleague the hon. member for Yale, a former Minister of National Defence. I should like to complete this record of distinguished personages who have played a part in drawing up and dealing with this bill by mentioning my fellow townsman, Commander Horace Read, R.C.N.V.R., of Amherst, Nova Scotia, who has had a distinguished career in the legal profession; who was a professor at Dalhousie college and who, because of his high qualifications, was secured to head the department of legislation in the law school at the university of Minnesota. He returned to Canada in order to contribute his services to- the naval department, and I believe was largely responsible for the drafting of this bill as well as other very important work. He also had a distinguished career in the last war, first enlisting in (he 219th battalion and later transferring to the air force. Those were early, pioneering days in the air, as compared with the period through which we are now passing.
I might also mention, as among the distinguished personages to take part in our
proceedings to-night, my fellow townsman the Minister of National Defence. As we all know, he distinguished himself in the last war. Now he is carrying a very great burden in administering the Department of National Defence during this struggle and has assumed the additional responsibility of leading this house during the absence of the Prime Minister in Great Britain and, at times, since his return. It gives me very great gratification, Mr. Chairman, to make these additions to the record of which you were reminded by the leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NAVAL SERVICE ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS AND CONSOLIDATION-ADAPTATION OF UNITED KINGDOM NAVAL DISCIPLINE ACT, 1866
speechtext:
I do not know whether or not I am in order, but I should like to draw 
attention to the presence in the gallery of a naval rating. I do not know who he is, but he has been here throughout the discussion.

Section agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
